# Scientists

### André-Marie Ampère (1775-1836)

#### Background

* French mathematician and physicist, born on January 20, 1775, in Lyon, and died on June 10, 1836, in Marseille.  
* Regarded as one of the founders of electrodynamics, a field he named himself, which laid the foundation for the mathematical study of electricity and magnetism.  
* Came from a prosperous bourgeois family; his father, Jean-Jacques Ampère, was a merchant and admirer of Rousseau, whose ideas influenced his education.  
* Largely self-taught, Ampère became a tutor and later a professor, and his work marked a key transition toward a mathematical understanding of electricity and magnetism.

#### nventions

* No major mechanical invention like a battery is directly attributed to Ampère, but he is credited with significant conceptual innovations.  
* Developed the idea of the solenoid, a term he coined, proposed early telegraph concepts, and designed various electrodynamic devices.  
* His work laid the foundation for current-measuring instruments such as the galvanometer and advanced the formal understanding of electrical circuits.

#### Discoveries & Laws

* Formulated Ampère’s Law, stating that the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop is proportional to the current passing through it.  
* Demonstrated that two parallel conductors carrying currents attract when flowing in the same direction and repel when in opposite directions—forming the physical basis of the ampere, the unit of electric current.  
* Developed the force law of two current elements, describing magnetic forces between infinitesimal current segments.  
* Proposed the existence of molecular currents, tiny circulating currents within matter that explain the microscopic origin of magnetism.  
* Coined the term “electrodynamics” and unified electricity and magnetism into a single, coherent field of study.

#### Works Published

* Published works include *Essai sur la Philosophie des Sciences, ou Exposition analytique d’une classification naturelle de toutes les connaissances humaines* (Paris, 1834–1843).  
* Authored *Description d’un appareil électro-dynamique construit* (Paris, 1824\) and *Mémoires sur l’électromagnétisme et l’électrodynamique* (Paris, 1921 edition).  
* Wrote *Exposé méthodique des phénomènes électro-dynamiques et des lois de ces phénomènes* (Paris, 1822\) and *Considérations sur la théorie mathématique du jeu* (Lyon, 1802).  
* Published *Mémoire sur la théorie mathématique des phénomènes électro-dynamiques uniquement déduite de l’expérience* (Paris, 1827).  
* Posthumous works include *Journal et correspondance* (Paris, 1872).

#### Context & Influence

* Expanded on Ørsted’s 1820 discovery that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, transforming it into a full theory of interaction between currents.  
* Laid the foundations for field theory and circuit analysis, influencing later scientists such as Maxwell.  
* Unified electricity and magnetism through his conceptual framework, paving the way for the modern science of electromagnetism.

#### Legacy & Recognition

* The SI unit of electric current, the ampere (A), is named in his honor.  
* His name is inscribed among the 72 great French scientists on the Eiffel Tower.  
* The Musée Ampère (Maison Ampère) in Poleymieux-au-Mont-d’Or commemorates his life and contributions.  
* Widely regarded as the father of electrodynamics.

#### Modern Connections

* Work underlies modern electromagnetic field theory, electromechanical systems, inductors and solenoids, and circuit design.  
* Provided the conceptual basis for the modern (2019) redefinition of the ampere, now defined by the fundamental charge, yet rooted in his original experiments on current-carrying conductors.

### Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (1824-1887)

**Background**

* Gustav Robert Kirchhoff was born on 12 March 1824 in Königsberg, Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia) and died on 17 October 1887 in Berlin, Germany.  
* A German physicist, he made foundational contributions to circuit theory, spectroscopy, thermal radiation, and graph theory.  
* Entered academia early, publishing his first significant papers around 1845 while still a graduate student.

**Inventions**

* Co-invented the first spectroscope with Robert Bunsen, enabling the discovery of new elements through their spectral lines.  
* Developed key formulas and laws in circuit theory and thermal radiation, shaping the foundation of modern electrical and optical physics.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Formulated Kirchhoff’s Circuit Laws (1845)  
  * Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL): the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it.  
  * Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL): the algebraic sum of potential differences in any closed loop is zero.  
* Extended Ohm’s Law to complex circuits containing multiple loops and junctions.  
* With Robert Bunsen, discovered the elements cesium (1860) and rubidium (1861) through spectral analysis, establishing that each chemical element emits and absorbs light at specific wavelengths.  
* Formulated Kirchhoff’s Law of Thermal Radiation (1859–1861), linking emission and absorption properties of materials.  
* Showed that an electrical signal in an ideal resistanceless wire would travel at the speed of light (1857).  
* Developed the matrix tree theorem in graph theory, also known as Kirchhoff’s Theorem.

**Works Published**

* Important works include *Chemical Analysis by Spectral Observations* (with Bunsen, 1860\) in *Annalen der Physik und Chemie*.  
* Authored a series of papers beginning in 1845 on circuit theory and electrical conduction.  
* Published studies on thermal radiation (1859) and their experimental proof (1861).  
* First paper appeared at age 21 in *Annalen der Physik und Chemie*.

**Context & Influence**

* Made possible the systematic analysis of telegraph circuits, power distribution systems, and electrical networks in the 19th century through Kirchhoff’s laws.  
* Created a vital link between physics and chemistry through spectroscopy, establishing the foundation for astrophysics and quantum mechanics.  
* Formulation of the thermal radiation law directly influenced Planck’s quantum hypothesis, marking a turning point in modern physics.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Honored in circuit theory, spectroscopy, and thermal physics for his pioneering contributions.  
* The Bunsen–Kirchhoff Award for Spectroscopy bears his name in recognition of his achievements.  
* Regarded as a founding figure of both electrical engineering and modern physics.

**Modern Connections**

* Contributions underpin electrical network analysis (including node and loop methods), transmission line theory, and component modelling.  
* Laid the foundation for spectroscopic techniques used in astronomy and chemistry, as well as thermal radiation modelling in modern physics.

**Alessandro Volta (1745–1827)**

**Background**

* Alessandro Volta, an Italian physicist and chemist, was a pioneer of electrochemistry.  
* Provided the first continuous source of electric current, marking a breakthrough in the study of electricity.  
* His rivalry with Luigi Galvani over “animal electricity” led him to demonstrate that electricity could arise from metal contact rather than biological sources.

**Inventions**

* Constructed the Voltaic pile (1800), composed of alternating zinc and copper plates separated by brine-soaked disks, providing the first steady electric current and enabling sustained electrical experimentation.  
* Developed the hydrogen lamp, demonstrating hydrogen combustion produced from zinc and sulfuric acid.  
* Invented the electrophorus (1775), a reusable static electricity generator based on electrostatic induction.  
* Created the first electromotive series, ranking metals by voltage potential, a precursor to modern standard electrode potentials.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* First to isolate methane (1776) and demonstrate that methane–air mixtures could be ignited by an electric spark, establishing the principle behind internal combustion.  
* Identified contact electricity at the junctions of dissimilar metals and distinguished between metallic and electrolytic conduction.  
* Established that the potential of a capacitor is directly proportional to its electric charge, forming a key concept in electrostatics.

**Works Published**

* First electromotive series (earliest tabulation of metal potentials).

**Context & Influence**

* Shifted the study of electricity from static to dynamic phenomena.  
* The voltaic pile replaced Leyden jars and friction machines as the primary experimental source, enabling breakthroughs in electrolysis, electrochemistry, and electromagnetism.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Volt (V) named in his honor; awarded the title of Count by Napoleon; commemorated at the Tempio Voltiano in Como.

 **Modern Connections**

* Foundations of battery chemistry, electrode potential theory, lithium-ion and fuel-cell design.

**Georg Simon Ohm (1789–1854)**

**Background**

* German physicist who quantified relations among voltage, current, and resistance; worked with limited resources and handmade apparatus; initially faced official skepticism before recognition.

**Inventions**

* No specific device attribution in the sources; built and refined his own experimental apparatus, galvanometers, and thermocouple-based arrangements to measure potential and current accurately.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Ohm’s law (V \= IR): current proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance; framed current flow with the water-through-a-pipe analogy; developed early resistivity and conduction insights; extended analysis to acoustics and harmonic vibrations.

**Works Published**

* Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet (1827) presenting the mathematical framework for circuits and the V-I-R relationship.

**Context & Influence**

* Made electricity a quantitative, calculable science suitable for analysis and engineering; generalized relationships that later underpin network methods.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Ohm (Ω) named for him; “ohmic conductor” terminology; cornerstone of circuit theory and electrical engineering.

**Modern Connections**

* Basis for circuit analysis, SPICE-class simulators, semiconductor and resistor network modeling, and power/energy calculations.

**André-Marie Ampère (1775–1836)**

**Background**

* French mathematician and physicist; born in Lyon, died in Marseille; self-educated polymath whose work founded electrodynamics; transitioned electricity and magnetism toward mathematical physics.

**Inventions**

* Conceptualized the solenoid and electrodynamic apparatus; laid groundwork for current-measuring devices (galvanometer) and early telegraph concepts.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Ampère’s Law: the line integral of magnetic field around a closed loop is proportional to the current enclosed; demonstrated forces between parallel current-carrying conductors (attraction for same-direction currents, repulsion for opposite), providing the physical basis for the unit of current; developed the force law of two current elements for magnetic interaction between infinitesimal current segments; proposed molecular currents as the microscopic origin of magnetism; coined the term electrodynamics; helped unify electricity and magnetism into a coherent field.

**Works Published**

* Exposé méthodique des phénomènes électro-dynamiques et des lois de ces phénomènes; Mémoire sur la théorie mathématique des phénomènes électro-dynamiques uniquement déduite de l’expérience; Description d’un appareil électro-dynamique construit; Essai sur la Philosophie des Sciences; Considérations sur la théorie mathématique du jeu; collected Mémoires and correspondence in later editions.

**Context & Influence**

* Built directly on Ørsted’s 1820 discovery of current deflecting a compass needle; converted qualitative effects into a general quantitative theory of interacting currents; strongly influenced Maxwell’s later synthesis.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Ampere (A) named for him; among the 72 scientists inscribed on the Eiffel Tower; commemorated at Maison/Musée Ampère; widely regarded as the father of electrodynamics.

**Modern Connections**

* Conceptual basis for modern field theory, solenoids, inductors, electromechanical force calculations, and the 2019 SI definition of the ampere based on the elementary charge.

**Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (1736–1806)**

**Background**

* French military engineer turned physicist; pioneer in precision measurement using torsion instruments.

**Inventions**

* Designed the torsion balance for microforce measurements that enabled quantitative electrostatics and magnetism.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Coulomb’s law (law of electrostatic force): electrostatic force proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of separation; confirmed an inverse-square relation for magnetic poles; distinguished conductors and insulators; showed charge resides on the surface of conductors and distributes by geometry; developed classical studies of torsion and the Coulomb law of friction in mechanics.

**Works Published**

* Not specified in the provided references beyond his experimental memoirs reported through the Academy.

**Context & Influence**

* Provided a rigorous quantitative foundation for electrostatics before the dynamic era of electricity sparked by Volta and Ørsted.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Coulomb (C) named for him; Coulomb’s constant appears in electrostatic formulas; set metrological standards for precision in 18th–19th century physics.

**Modern Connections**

* Coulomb potential central to atomic physics and quantum chemistry; ubiquitous in electrostatic modeling from molecules to devices.

**Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (1824–1887)**

**Background**

* German physicist born in Königsberg and active in Berlin; foundational contributions in circuit theory, spectroscopy, thermal radiation, and even graph theory.

**Inventions**

* Co-invented with Bunsen a practical spectroscope for element identification by spectral lines; formalized circuit analysis procedures that function as conceptual instrumentation for networks.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Kirchhoff’s Circuit Laws (1845): KCL stating the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving; KVL stating the algebraic sum of potential differences in any closed loop is zero; extended Ohm’s law to multi-loop and multi-node networks; demonstrated electrical signals propagate at light speed in conductors; formulated Kirchhoff’s law of thermal radiation (1859–1861); with Bunsen pioneered the identification of the elements in the Sun and discovered cesium (1860) and rubidium (1861) by spectroscopy; established that each element has characteristic emission/absorption lines; contributed Kirchhoff’s (matrix tree) theorem in graph theory.

**Works Published**

* Chemical Analysis by Spectral Observations (with Bunsen); early circuit theory papers beginning 1845; thermal radiation papers of 1859 and their proofs in 1861; numerous Annalen der Physik und Chemie publications.

**Context & Influence**

* Enabled systematic analysis of telegraph and power circuits; spectroscopy bridged physics and chemistry and catalyzed astrophysics and quantum theory; thermal radiation results paved the way to Planck’s quantization.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Enduring centrality in circuit network analysis and spectroscopy; Bunsen-Kirchhoff Award for spectroscopy bears his and Bunsen’s names; regarded as a founder of electrical engineering and modern physics methods.

**Modern Connections**

* Node/loop analysis, transmission-line and power distribution modeling, spectroscopic diagnostics in astronomy and chemistry, and thermal radiation modeling in physics and engineering.

**Michael Faraday (1791–1867)**

**Background**

* British, largely self-taught experimentalist; apprenticed bookbinder; long-time Royal Institution lecturer; declined knighthood and state burial.

**Inventions**

* Electric motor (1821) demonstrating rotation from current and a magnetic pole.   
* Electromagnetic induction (1831) establishing that changing magnetic flux induces emf, basis of generators and transformers  
* Faraday cage (1836) demonstrating surface charge and interior shielding  
* Gas liquefaction and early refrigeration cycles.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Dielectric constant, found using simple electrostatic apparatus (spherical capacitors), the capacitance increase by a numerical factor $\kappa$  
* Discovered electromagnetic rotation using a mercury bath.  
* Faraday’s law of induction: induced emf proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux.  
* Faraday’s laws of electrolysis, forming the foundation of electrochemistry.  
* Discovered diamagnetism.  
* Introduced field and lines of force.  
* Faraday effect linking magnetism and light via polarization rotation  
* Discovered benzene (1825).

**Works Published**

* A Chemical History of a Candle; Burn: Michael Faraday’s Candle; The Chemical History of a Candle, a Course of Lectures Delivered Before a Juvenile Audience at the Royal Institution; Scientific Papers: Physics, Chemistry, Astronomy, Geology.

**Context & Influence**

* His experimental field concepts directly inspired Maxwell’s theoretical unification of electromagnetism; his public lectures established a model for science communication.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Farad (F) and the Faraday constant recognize his contributions.

**Modern Connections**

* Principles behind motors, generators, transformers, MRI, wireless charging, and electromagnetic shielding.

**Nikola Tesla (1856–1943)**

**Background**

* Serbian-American inventor and electrical engineer; central to the War of Currents; advocated AC power distribution; worked for Edison, partnered with Westinghouse; later faced financial hardship.

**Inventions**

* Induction motor using alternating current and rotating magnetic fields with stator and rotor; polyphase AC systems enabling efficient long-distance transmission; Tesla coil with primary and secondary coils and a spark gap producing high-frequency, high-voltage discharges that can shoot visible “lightning,” pass currents through the body, and create electron winds; first successful wireless energy transfer to power devices in 1891; teleautomaton, a radio-controlled boat operating propeller and lights via radio waves, marking a first in remote control, one of the earliest robots, and a precursor to drones; devised practical AC distribution systems and emphasized that he did not invent AC but made it applicable at scale.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Advanced radio-frequency generation and reception; resonance and high-frequency AC phenomena; devised electrical distribution employing AC; wide experimentation in wireless communication and power.

**Works Published**

* My Inventions: The Autobiography of Nikola Tesla; The Fantastic Inventions of Nikola Tesla; The Problem of Increasing Human Energy; Experiments with Alternate Currents of High Potential and High Frequency; Inventions, Researches and Writings of Nikola Tesla.

**Context & Influence**

* Public demonstrations (including at the World’s Fair); patents adopted in Westinghouse AC systems; Wardenclyffe Tower attempted global wireless communication and power.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Tesla (T) as the SI unit of magnetic flux density; enduring public recognition; icon of AC electrification and wireless concepts.

**Modern Connections**

* Foundations for modern power grids, radio and RF systems, resonant wireless charging, and high-frequency technology; cultural and industrial legacy continued in Tesla, Inc.

**Heinrich Hertz (1857–1894)**

**Background**

* German physicist who experimentally verified Maxwell’s electromagnetic wave theory; initially considered his work to have no practical application.

**Inventions**

* Spark-gap transmitter and receiver and laboratory resonant circuits; dipole antenna; standing-wave setups for wavelength and wave-speed measurements.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* First controlled generation and detection of radio waves; proved propagation through air at light speed; observed the photoelectric effect; studied how different materials interact in electrical contact as noted in the provided material.

**Works Published**

* Ueber die Beziehungen zwischen Licht und Elektricität: Ein Vortrag gehalten bei der 62 Versammlung Deutscher Naturforscher und Aerzte in Heidelberg; Electric Waves; The Principles of Mechanics Presented in a New Form; Miscellaneous Papers.

**Context & Influence**

* Provided decisive experimental confirmation of Maxwell’s theory; directly enabled Marconi’s wireless telegraphy and the radio era.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Hertz (Hz) named for frequency; established radio physics as an experimental discipline.

**Modern Connections**

* Foundation of radio, radar, Wi-Fi, cellular systems, and all RF engineering.

**James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879)**

**Background**

* Scottish theoretical physicist who unified electricity, magnetism, and light.

**Inventions**

* None in the mechanical sense in the provided sources; principal contribution is theoretical formulation.

**Discoveries & Laws**

* Maxwell’s equations (1864–1865) integrating Faraday’s and Ampère’s results; displacement current completing the field equations; prediction that light is an electromagnetic wave.

**Works Published**

* Not specified in the provided references beyond his seminal papers; his Treatise and papers underpin the field.

**Context & Influence**

* Provided the mathematical foundation for Faraday’s field concept; set the stage for Hertz’s experiments and influenced Einstein’s development of modern physics.

**Legacy & Recognition**

* Regarded among the greatest physicists after Newton; his equations are the cornerstone of classical electromagnetism.

**Modern Connections**

* Basis for electromagnetic theory, antennas, optical fiber transmission, field simulation, and quantum electrodynamics.

**Types of Magnetism and Materials**

| Term | Definition | Cause (Atomic Level) | Response to External Magnetic Field | Strength | Examples |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Ferromagnetism | Strong, permanent magnetism due to parallel alignment of magnetic moments | Unpaired electron spins align spontaneously in domains | Strong attraction; can retain magnetization even after field is removed | Very strong | Iron (Fe), Nickel (Ni), Cobalt (Co), some alloys |
| Ferromagnetic Materials | Materials that exhibit ferromagnetism | Same as above | Strongly attracted to magnets; can be permanently magnetized | Very strong | Iron, steel, cobalt, nickel |
| Paramagnetism | Weak magnetism due to partial alignment of unpaired electron spins | Atoms/molecules with unpaired electrons | Weak attraction; disappears when field is removed | Weak | Aluminum, Platinum, Magnesium |
| Paramagnetic Materials | Materials that exhibit paramagnetism | Same as above | Weakly attracted to external fields; no permanent magnetization | Weak | Oxygen, tungsten, lithium |
| Diamagnetism | Universal weak repulsion due to induced currents opposing applied field | Paired electrons (no permanent magnetic moment) | Weak repulsion; disappears when field is removed | Very weak | Copper, Bismuth, Water, Graphite |
| Diamagnetic Materials | Materials that exhibit diamagnetism | Same as above | Repelled by magnets; cannot be permanently magnetized | Very weak | Gold, silver, lead |
| Antiferromagnetism | Neighboring spins align in opposite directions, canceling each other | Exchange interactions cause alternating spin alignment | No net magnetization; weak response | Moderate | Manganese oxide (MnO), Nickel oxide (NiO) |
| Ferrimagnetism | Opposite spin alignment but unequal magnitudes, leaving net magnetization | Different ions with unequal spins | Strong attraction; permanent magnetization possible | Strong (but less than ferromagnetism) | Magnetite (Fe₃O₄), ferrites |
| Superparamagnetism | Occurs in very small ferromagnetic/ferrimagnetic nanoparticles | Thermal fluctuations randomize magnetic moments | Behaves like paramagnet but with stronger response | Stronger than paramagnetism | Nanoparticles of iron oxide |
| Magnetic Domains | Regions in ferromagnetic/ferrimagnetic materials where spins align | Collective spin alignment | Domains grow/shrink under external field | Key to hysteresis | Iron, cobalt |
| Curie Temperature | Temperature above which ferromagnetic/ferrimagnetic materials lose magnetism | Thermal agitation disrupts spin alignment | Above this, material becomes paramagnetic | Material-specific | Iron: \~770°C |

**Wheatstone Bridge**

A wheatstone bridge is used to measure an unknown resistance value to a high degree of accuracy. It uses 4 resistors set up in a diamond fashion (shown below) and a voltmeter. In the schematic below, Rx is the unknown resistance, R1 and R3 are fixed resistance values (generally the same, but they don't have to be the same, also generally \>1% tolerance, but again, not always) and R2 is a variable resistor (potentiometer, this is not always the case, see below). By adjusting R2 until the voltmeter reads 0 volts, you know that the ratio between the R1/R2 and R3/Rx is equal.

To understand this, think of a circuit with two resistors of equal value in series, connected to a \+5v source, because the resistances are equal, the voltage drop is equal, this kind of circuit is called a voltage divider, because the voltage in between the two resistors is 1/2 the input voltage. Again, imagine a circuit with 2 resistors in series connected to a \+5v source, however this time, the resistors are 50 ohms and 25 ohms, because the total resistance is 75 ohms, at 5v, we can calculate the current, and from there calculate the voltage drop from each resistor, you should have gotten 3.33 volts across the first, and 1.66 for the second one; the voltage happens to be in the same ratio as the resistance values; now that we've proved that, we can apply it to the wheatstone bridge.

With that in mind, we now know that the ratio of the resistors is what controls the voltage at the midpoint, so if two sets of resistors have the same ratio, then they would have the same voltage. When the voltage across the bridge is 0, the sets of resistors (R1/R2 and R3/Rx) have the same voltage, and thus the same ratio of resistance values\! Since we know the ratio of the first leg (R1/R2, remember we set R2 to a known value to balance the bridge) and we know R3, it's fairly simple to solve for Rx.

What if you don't want to have to change R2? Then, using the same principle, you can take the voltage across the bridge, and calculate Rx from that. Basically, by applying all the concepts discussed here (Kirchhoff's laws, Ohm's law, etc) you end up at the equation  
${V}_{G}=\frac{{R}_{x}}{{R}_{3}+{R}_{x}}-\frac{{R}_{2}}{{R}_{1}+{R}_{2}}$

Pure mathematical proof:  
${V}_{G}=0$	${V}_{D}={V}_{B}$  
Then ${V}_{1}={V}_{3}$, ${V}_{2}={V}_{x}$  
Thus, $\frac{{V}_{R1}}{{V}_{R2}}=\frac{{V}_{R3}}{{V}_{R4}}$  
$\frac{{I}_{R1R2}{R}_{1}}{{I}_{R1R2}{R}_{2}}=\frac{{I}_{R3Rx}{R}_{3}}{{I}_{R3Rx}{R}_{x}}$  
$\frac{{R}_{1}}{{R}_{2}}=\frac{{R}_{3}}{{R}_{x}}$  
${R}_{x}={R}_{3}(\frac{{R}_{2}}{{R}_{1}})$  
For voltage across the galvanometer in an unbalanced wheatstone bridge:  
${V}_{G}={V}_{2}-{V}_{x}$  
${V}_{G}={I}_{R1R2}{R}_{2}-{I}_{R3Rx}{R}_{x}=$

**AC Generator/Alternator**  
If a machine is constructed to rotate a [magnetic field](https://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/direct-current/chpt-15/magnetic-fields-and-inductance/) around a set of stationary wire coils with the turning of a shaft, AC voltage will be produced across the wire coils as that shaft is rotated, in accordance with Faraday’s Law of [electromagnetic induction](https://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/direct-current/chpt-14/electromagnetic-induction/).  
**![][image3]**  
**![][image4]**  
**![][image5]**  
An instrument called an ***oscilloscope***, Figure below, is used to display a changing voltage over time on a graphical screen. You may be familiar with the appearance of an *ECG* or *EKG* (electrocardiograph) machine, used by physicians to graph the oscillations of a patient’s heart over time.

The ECG is a special-purpose oscilloscope expressly designed for medical use. General-purpose oscilloscopes have the ability to display voltage from virtually any voltage source, plotted as a graph with time as the independent variable.

**![][image6]**  
**![][image7]**  
If we average all the points on a sine waveform algebraically (that is, to consider their *sign*, either positive or negative), the average value for most waveforms is technically zero, because all the positive points cancel out all the negative points over a full cycle. This, of course, will be true for any waveform having equal-area portions above and below the “zero” line of a plot. However, as a *practical* measure of a waveform’s aggregate value, “average” is usually defined as the mathematical mean of all the points’ *absolute values* over a cycle.  
![][image8]![][image9]

In addition to RMS, average, peak (crest), and peak-to-peak measures of an AC waveform, there are ratios expressing the proportionality between some of these fundamental measurements. The ***crest factor*** of an AC waveform, for instance, is the ratio of its peak (crest) value divided by its RMS value.

The ***form factor*** of an AC waveform is the ratio of its RMS value divided by its average value. Square-shaped waveforms always have crest and form factors equal to 1, since the peak is the same as the RMS and average values. Sinusoidal waveforms have an RMS value of 0.707 (the reciprocal of the square root of 2\) and a form factor of 1.11 (0.707/0.636).

Triangle- and sawtooth-shaped waveforms have RMS values of 0.577 (the reciprocal of square root of 3\) and form factors of 1.15 (0.577/0.5).

***Arbitrary waveforms have no simple conversions.***

This is a very important concept to understand when using an **analog D’Arsonval meter movement** to measure AC voltage or current. An analog D’Arsonval movement, calibrated to indicate sine-wave RMS amplitude, will only be accurate when measuring pure sine waves.

If the waveform of the voltage or current being measured is anything but a pure sine wave, the indication given by the meter will not be the true RMS value of the waveform, because the degree of needle deflection in an analog D’Arsonval meter movement is proportional to the *average* value of the waveform, not the RMS.

RMS meter calibration is obtained by “skewing” the span of the meter so that it displays a small multiple of the average value, which will be equal to be the RMS value for a particular waveshape and *a particular waveshape only*.

Since the sine-wave shape is most common in electrical measurements, it is the waveshape assumed for analog meter calibration, and the small multiple used in the calibration of the meter is 1.1107 (the form factor: 0.707/0.636: the ratio of RMS divided by average for a sinusoidal waveform).

Any waveshape other than a pure sine wave will have a different ratio of RMS and average values, and thus a meter calibrated for sine-wave voltage or current will not indicate true RMS when reading a non-sinusoidal wave. Bear in mind that this limitation applies only to simple, analog AC meters not employing “True-RMS” technology.

All measurements of AC voltage and current must be expressed in the same terms (peak, peak-to-peak, average, or RMS). If the source voltage is given in peak AC volts, then all currents and voltages subsequently calculated are cast in terms of peak units. Unless otherwise stated, all values of voltage and current in AC circuits are generally assumed to be RMS rather than peak, average, or peak-to-peak.

**Light Emitting Diodes**  
Unlike normal signal diodes which are made for detection or power rectification, and which are made from either Germanium or Silicon semiconductor materials, Light Emitting Diodes are made from exotic semiconductor compounds, all mixed together at different ratios to produce a distinct wavelength of colour.   
![][image10]

# TO DO

**Diode Voltage Drop & Basic Info**

| Name | ${V}_{on}$ | ${V}_{breakdown}$ | Material | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Germanium diode (signal) | \~0.3V | 20-100V | Germanium (Ge), lightly doped to form a PN junction. | Low-voltage signal detection and radio-frequency applications due to low forward voltage. |
| Silicon diode (rectifier / signal) | 0.6-0.7V |  | Silicon (Si) semiconductor doped into P and N regions. | General rectification, power conversion, and signal protection in most electronic circuits. |
| Schottky diode (Si) | 0.15-0.4V |  | Silicon (Si) forming a junction with a metal (usually Al, Pt, Mo, or Ti). | Fast switching and low-forward-voltage rectification, commonly used in power electronics and high-speed digital circuits. |
| Silicon Carbide (SiC) power diode | 3.0V |  | Silicon Carbide (SiC), typically 4H-SiC polytype, with P and N doping. | High-voltage, high-temperature, high-efficiency power rectification. |
| Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) diode | 1.2V |  | Gallium Arsenide (GaAs), a III–V compound semiconductor with P- and N-type doping. | High-frequency, microwave, and optoelectronic applications (photodiodes, fast detectors). |
| Laser diode | 1.2V (red typical; varies with color) |  | III–V compound semiconductors such as GaAs, GaAsP, InGaAs, GaN, or InGaN in quantum-well layers. | Coherent light generation for communication, sensing, optical storage, and illumination. |
| Zenner diode | 0.7V forward, breakdown at rated Zener voltage (e.g., 3.3V, 5.1V) |  | Silicon (Si) PN junction specially doped for controlled reverse breakdown. | Maintains a stable, precise reference voltage in reverse bias, used in voltage regulators, protection circuits, and shunt references. |
| Avalanche diode | 0.7V forward, high reverse breakdown (50–400V typical) |  | Silicon (Si) or Silicon Carbide (SiC) PN junction engineered for uniform avalanche conduction. | Provides controlled high-voltage breakdown for surge suppression, over-voltage protection, and stable high-voltage references. |
| LED | Color-dependent (see below) |  | III–V semiconductors such as GaAs, GaP, GaAsP, InGaN, or AlGaInP with doped PN junctions. | Emits light via electron-hole recombination; used in displays, indicators, illumination, signaling, and optical transmission. |
| Photodiode | 0.5–0.7V forward (operates mostly in reverse bias) |  | Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), or Indium Gallium Arsenide (InGaAs) with PN or PIN structures. | Converts incident light into electrical current with high sensitivity; used in cameras, detectors, fiber-optic receivers, and solar cells. |
| PIN diode | 1.0V |  | Silicon (Si) with a P-doped layer, an intrinsic (undoped) layer, and an N-doped layer. | Provides a wide depletion region with low capacitance and fast switching; used as an RF attenuator, RF switch, and in high-frequency modulators. |
| Tunnel diode (Esaki diode) | 0.1–0.3V |  | Heavily doped Germanium (Ge) or Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) creating an extremely thin PN junction. | Exhibits quantum tunneling and negative resistance, enabling ultra-fast switching and microwave oscillation applications. |
| Varactor (Varicap) diode | 0.7V |  | Silicon (Si) PN junction engineered for voltage-dependent junction capacitance. | Acts as a voltage-controlled capacitor for RF tuning, frequency modulation, and voltage-controlled oscillators (VCOs). |
| Step-Recovery Diode (SRD) | 0.7V |  | Silicon (Si) PN junction optimized for abrupt reverse recovery charge removal. | Generates sharp pulses and rich harmonic spectra, used in frequency multipliers, pulse generators, and microwave circuits. |
| Gunn diode | N/A (not a PN junction) |  | Bulk Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) or Indium Phosphide (InP) exhibiting the transferred-electron effect. | Generates microwave oscillations without a PN junction; used in radar sensors, motion detectors, and microwave transmitters. |
| IMPATT diode (Impact Ionization Avalanche Transit Time diode) | \~7–20V reverse breakdown |  | Silicon (Si), Gallium Arsenide (GaAs), or Silicon Carbide (SiC) with avalanche layers. | Produces high-power microwave signals via impact ionization and avalanche transit time effects; used in radar and RF transmitters. |
| TRAPATT diode (Trapped Plasma Avalanche Triggered Transit) | \~7–20V reverse breakdown |  | Silicon (Si) avalanche structure (variant of IMPATT). | Generates very high microwave power with high efficiency using trapped plasma avalanche mechanisms. |
| BARITT diode ([Barrier Injection Transit Time](https://www.google.com/search?q=Barrier+Injection+Transit+Time&sca_esv=f428b6d1b594cc50&sxsrf=AE3TifPY5i4juktTn9Dcq6I0z2OIvphLtg%3A1762548227715&ei=A1oOaY2wK-S0qtsP7ubQ4AE&ved=2ahUKEwjTx_Pp8-CQAxVTk2oFHZFoFY8QgK4QegQIARAC&uact=5&oq=BARITT+diode+full+name&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiFkJBUklUVCBkaW9kZSBmdWxsIG5hbWUyBhAAGBYYHjIFEAAY7wUyCBAAGIAEGKIEMggQABiiBBiJBUjxCVAAWIkJcAB4AZABAJgBXqABoQeqAQIxMbgBA8gBAPgBAZgCC6AC7AfCAgUQABiABMICCxAAGIAEGIYDGIoFwgIFECEYoAHCAgUQIRirApgDAJIHAzkuMqAH5iayBwM5LjK4B-wHwgcHMC4yLjguMcgHMA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&safe=active&ssui=on&mstk=AUtExfBUd8RGNHraql5HcldADNA9mZQQEcwSk8seLgE6J-IBtW46wSL7OcXNiTKnphykl9RJjHbvBBjDJhmlelhst0MVIQRU3vxBx2oPvPZX2OmeaxTNrRS2Dvhddnty5acuifM0UOVggR9yl0dIzqSygDoQ8KOdzB9HLbZ-IGx-kXzm4CWm5gWW_-FRpXI_wW2v88YuqscaP7rBmY9ShyD7H2nLyIdqP1jLDFb_bqDrjBkGGlygS7gFz6__NGD-8X8VLuzopeh1GxAMI53Gkmo2zrKM&csui=3) diode) | \~2–8V reverse breakdown |  | Silicon (Si) bipolar diode with specially designed injection regions. | Low-noise microwave source using barrier-injection transit-time effects; used in RF oscillators. |

**N-type doping:** Adds atoms with extra electrons (e.g., phosphorus in Si), creating mobile negative charge carriers (electrons).  
**P-type doping:** Adds atoms with fewer electrons (e.g., boron in Si), creating mobile positive charge carriers (“holes”).

**LED Materials and Characteristics**

| Material | Description | Important Characteristics |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) | Infrared and early red LEDs; efficient IR emission. | **Direct bandgap**, emits **850–940 nm**, high IR efficiency, used in remotes & sensors. |
| Gallium Phosphide (GaP) | Older-generation red, yellow, green LEDs (low brightness). | **Indirect bandgap**, low efficiency, emits **560–700 nm**, requires heavy doping to improve output. |
| Gallium Arsenide Phosphide (GaAsP) | Red, orange, yellow LEDs with tunable bandgap. | Adjustable emission **580–700 nm**, efficiency increases with higher As content, used in indicators. |
| Gallium Nitride (GaN) | Base material for blue, green, UV LEDs. | **Wide bandgap (3.4 eV)**, emits **365–480 nm**, high power capability; used for high-brightness LEDs. |
| Gallium Indium Nitride (GaInN / InGaN) | Modern high-brightness blue, green, and white LEDs. | Composition-tunable; emits **380–520 nm**, enables phosphor-based white LEDs; extremely high efficiency. |
| Aluminum Gallium Arsenide (AlGaAs) | High-efficiency red and IR emitters. | **Direct bandgap**, emits **650–900 nm**, high radiative efficiency; used in IR communication. |
| Aluminum Gallium Indium Phosphide (AlGaInP) | Bright red, orange, yellow LEDs; dominant red-LED tech. | Very high efficiency, emits **560–650 nm**, forms double-heterostructures for strong confinement. |
| Aluminum Gallium Nitride (AlGaN) | UV-A/B/C LEDs. | **Extremely wide bandgap**, emits **210–365 nm**, used for sterilization and sensors; efficiency decreases at deep UV. |
| Aluminum Nitride (AlN) | Deep UV emission and substrate material. | Bandgap **6.2 eV**, emits **200–220 nm**, excellent thermal conductivity; often used as a GaN substrate. |
| Indium Gallium Phosphide (InGaP) | Efficient red–orange LEDs. | Direct bandgap; emits **580–650 nm**, high brightness at low power. |
| Indium Phosphide (InP) | Infrared LEDs and photonics. | Direct bandgap; emits **920–1600 nm**, used in telecom and optical detectors. |
| Indium Nitride (InN) | Near-IR to deep-red emission; mostly experimental. | Very narrow bandgap (**0.7 eV**), emits **1.5–2.1 μm**, used mostly in InGaN band engineering. |
| Zinc Selenide (ZnSe) | Early blue LED material; now largely replaced. | Direct bandgap (**2.7 eV**), emits **blue 460–480 nm**, low durability compared to GaN. |
| Zinc Sulfide (ZnS) | Early EL material; weak LED emission. | Emission **450–550 nm**, low efficiency, used in EL panels and phosphors. |
| Cadmium Selenide (CdSe) | Quantum-dot LEDs (QLEDs). | Emits **480–650 nm** depending on dot size; **very narrow linewidth**; extremely high color purity. |
| Cadmium Sulfide (CdS) | QD and thin-film LED material. | Emits **500–550 nm**, good for green QDs; used in research and photodetectors. |
| Silicon Carbide (SiC) | First blue LEDs; now used as substrate. | Very wide bandgap (**3.0 eV**), emits **blue/UV**, very low efficiency compared to GaN. |
| Silicon (Si) | Weak IR electroluminescence (not used for visible LEDs). | **Indirect bandgap**, extremely low efficiency; emits **IR \~1150 nm** only in specialized devices. |
| Organic LED Materials (OLED) — e.g., Alq₃ | Organic molecules emitting light by exciton recombination. | Tunable color, flexible, low power, but lower lifetime; used in displays and lighting. |
| Perovskites — e.g., CsPbBr₃, MAPbI₃ | High-brightness, next-gen LEDs with tunable emission. | Extremely narrow emission peaks, tunable **400–700 nm**, very high efficiency (lab), moisture-sensitive. |

**ELECTRICAL COMPONENTS**  
**RESISTORS**  
 Properties: Resistors oppose current flow and convert electrical energy into heat. They are passive components with no gain.  
 Units: Ohms (Ω).  
 Parameters:

* Resistance (R) – opposition to current, R \= V/I.

* Tolerance – accuracy (±1%, ±5%, ±10%).

* Power rating (W) – how much heat it can safely dissipate.

* Temperature coefficient – change in resistance per degree Celsius (ppm/°C).  
   Types:

* **Carbon Film**: Cheap, general-purpose, moderate tolerance (\~5%). Used in basic circuits.

* **Metal Film**: Precise, low noise, tight tolerance (\~1%). Used in audio or precision circuits.

* **Wirewound**: High-power applications, inductive behavior may limit high-frequency use.

* **Potentiometers/Trimmers**: Variable resistors; adjust voltage dividers, tuning circuits.

* **Thermistors**: Resistance changes with temperature (NTC: decreases with heat, PTC: increases).

* **Photoresistors (LDRs)**: Resistance changes with light intensity.  
   Applications: Current limiting (LEDs), voltage dividers, transistor biasing, pull-up/pull-down in logic circuits, sensors (thermistors/LDRs).

---

**CAPACITORS**  
 Properties: Store energy in an electric field, oppose sudden voltage changes. Passive component.  
 Units: Farads (F).  
 Parameters: Capacitance (C), Voltage rating (V), Equivalent Series Resistance (ESR), leakage current, tolerance, dielectric type.  
 Types:

* **Ceramic**: Small capacitance, high-frequency applications, stable, non-polarized.

* **Electrolytic**: Large capacitance, polarized, used in power supply filtering, low-frequency applications.

* **Tantalum**: Small, stable, polarized, low leakage, higher cost.

* **Film**: Precise, low loss, non-polarized, used in audio or timing circuits.

* **Supercapacitors**: Very high capacitance, backup energy storage, slow charge/discharge.  
   Applications: Filtering (power supply smoothing), coupling AC signals, decoupling (bypassing), timing circuits, oscillators, energy storage.

---

**INDUCTORS**  
 Properties: Store energy in magnetic field, oppose changes in current. Passive component.  
 Units: Henry (H).  
 Parameters: Inductance (L), DC resistance (DCR), saturation current, Q factor, self-resonant frequency.  
 Types:

* **Air-Core**: No magnetic core, linear, high-frequency use.

* **Iron-Core/Ferrite-Core**: High inductance, used in power supplies, transformers.  
   Applications: Filters (chokes), tuning circuits, transformers, energy storage in switching power supplies, RF applications.

---

**DIODES**  
 Properties: Conduct current primarily in one direction, block reverse current. Active component.  
 Units: Voltage (V), Current (A).  
 Parameters: Forward voltage drop (Vf), Maximum forward current (If), Reverse breakdown voltage (Vr), Reverse recovery time.  
 Types:

* **Standard Silicon**: Vf \~0.6–0.7V, rectification.

* **Schottky**: Vf \~0.2–0.4V, fast switching, low voltage drop.

* **Zener**: Operates in reverse breakdown; used for voltage regulation.

* **LEDs (Light Emitting Diodes)**: Emit light, forward voltage depends on color, current-limited by resistor.

* **Photodiodes**: Convert light to current, often reverse-biased for detection.  
   Applications: Rectifiers, voltage regulation, signal demodulation, indicators, logic isolation.

---

**TRANSISTORS**  
 Properties: Semiconductor devices that amplify or switch signals. Active components.  
 Types:

* **BJT (Bipolar Junction Transistor)**: Current-controlled; NPN or PNP.

  * NPN: Current flows from collector to emitter when base is positive relative to emitter.

  * PNP: Current flows from emitter to collector when base is negative relative to emitter.

  * Parameters: Current gain (hFE), max collector current (Ic), max collector-emitter voltage (Vce).

  * Applications: Amplifiers, switches, oscillators, digital logic.

* **FET (Field Effect Transistor)**: Voltage-controlled; JFET or MOSFET.

  * Parameters: Threshold voltage (Vth), Rds(on) for MOSFET, max current and voltage.

  * Applications: Switches, amplifiers, high-input-impedance circuits.

---

**INTEGRATED CIRCUITS (ICs)**  
 Properties: Combine multiple components (transistors, resistors, capacitors) into a single package. Active components.  
 Types:

* **Analog ICs**: Operational amplifiers (op-amps), voltage regulators, comparators.

  * Op-Amps: High-gain differential amplifiers. Applications: signal amplification, summing, filtering, active filters, integrators, differentiators. Key parameters: Gain, bandwidth, input/output impedance, slew rate, offset voltage.

* **Digital ICs**: Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR), flip-flops, counters, microcontrollers.

* **Mixed-Signal ICs**: ADCs, DACs, PWM controllers.  
   Applications: Signal processing, computation, embedded systems, automation, sensor interfacing.

---

**SWITCHES**  
 Properties: Mechanically/electronically open or close circuits.  
 Types: SPST, SPDT, DPDT, Toggle, Push-button, Rotary, Slide.  
 Parameters: Current rating, voltage rating, contact resistance, mechanical life.  
 Applications: Circuit control, user inputs, mode selection, reset, on/off switching.

---

**RELAYS**  
 Properties: Electrically operated switches; allow low-current control of high-current load. Active component.  
 Parameters: Coil voltage/current, contact rating, switching time, mechanical life.  
 Types: Electromechanical, Solid-State (SSR).  
 Applications: Automation, isolation, motor control, high-power switching.

---

**TRANSFORMERS**  
 Properties: Transfer energy between circuits magnetically; can step-up or step-down voltage. Passive component.  
 Parameters: Turns ratio, frequency range, power rating, efficiency, leakage inductance.  
 Applications: Power conversion, isolation, impedance matching, audio transformers, RF.

---

**FUSES AND CIRCUIT BREAKERS**  
 Properties: Overcurrent protection.  
 Parameters: Rated voltage/current, trip characteristics.  
 Applications: Prevent damage to circuits, protect against fire hazards, safeguard sensitive components.

---

**OSCILLATORS**  
 Properties: Generate periodic waveforms. Active component.  
 Types: RC, LC, Crystal, Quartz, Relaxation oscillators.  
 Parameters: Frequency, waveform type, stability, amplitude.  
 Applications: Clock sources for digital circuits, RF signal generation, timers, communication systems.

---

**SENSORS**  
 Properties: Convert physical stimuli into electrical signals.  
 Types & Examples:

* Temperature: Thermistor, Thermocouple.

* Light: Photodiode, LDR.

* Magnetic: Hall effect sensor.

* Motion: Accelerometer, Gyroscope.

* Pressure/Proximity/Touch.  
   Parameters: Sensitivity, range, accuracy, response time.  
   Applications: Feedback, monitoring, automation, IoT devices, safety systems.

---

**ACTUATORS**  
 Properties: Convert electrical signals into mechanical motion.  
 Types: DC motors, Stepper motors, Servo motors, Piezoelectric actuators.  
 Parameters: Voltage, current, torque, speed, step angle (stepper), position resolution (servo).  
 Applications: Robotics, motion control, pumps, fans, automated systems.

---

**CONNECTORS AND WIRES**  
 Properties: Provide physical and electrical connectivity.  
 Parameters: Current rating, voltage rating, insulation, wire gauge (AWG).  
 Applications: PCB interconnections, modular assemblies, power/signal transmission.

---

**POWER SOURCES**  
 Types: Batteries (Li-ion, Alkaline, NiMH), AC mains, DC power supplies, Solar panels.  
 Parameters: Voltage, current capability, ripple, stability, internal resistance.  
 Applications: Power electronics, portable devices, embedded systems, lab testing.

---

**MISCELLANEOUS COMPONENTS**

* **Crystals**: Frequency reference, stable oscillator.

* **Varistors**: Surge protection, voltage-dependent resistance.

* **Optocouplers**: Electrical isolation via light.

* **Voltage Regulators**: Linear or switching; maintain stable voltage.

* **Memory ICs**: SRAM, DRAM, EEPROM, Flash.

* **Displays**: Seven-segment, LCD, OLED for numerical/text/graphic output.

**Common Terms**

| Term | Field | Definition | Key Distinction / Notes |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Electric Charge | Electrostatics | Property of matter that causes it to experience a force in an electric field; can be positive or negative. | Fundamental unit; unlike mass, it comes in discrete values (multiples of electron charge). |
| Coulomb’s Law | Electrostatics | Force between two point charges: $F=\frac{k{q}_{1}{q}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}$ | Similar to Newton’s law of gravitation but can be attractive or repulsive. |
| Electric Field (E) | Electrostatics | Region around a charge where other charges experience force: E=F/q | Vector quantity; points away from positive charges, toward negative charges. |
| Electric Potential (V) | Electrostatics | Work done per unit charge to move a charge in an electric field. | Scalar; different from electric field (vector). Often confused. |
| Capacitance (C) | Circuits | Ability of a system to store charge per unit voltage: C=Q/V | Measured in farads; capacitors store energy in electric fields. |
| Resistance (R) | Circuits | Opposition to current flow: R=V/I | Measured in ohms; distinct from resistivity (material property). |
| Resistivity (ρ) | Circuits | Material property defining resistance per unit length and area. | Often confused with resistance; resistivity is intrinsic, resistance depends on geometry. |
| Current (I) | Circuits | Flow of electric charge per unit time. | Conventional current flows from \+ to –, opposite electron flow. |
| Magnetic Field (B) | Magnetism | Region where magnetic forces act; defined by force on moving charges: F=qvB | Vector; measured in tesla. Different from magnetic flux. |
| Magnetic Flux (Φ) | Magnetism | Measure of total magnetic field passing through a surface: Φ=B⋅A | Scalar; flux density is B. |
| Magnetic Flux Density (B) | Magnetism | Strength of magnetic field per unit area, also called magnetic induction. | Vector quantity; often confused with flux. Flux \= total field, density \= local intensity. |
| Magnetic Declination | Magnetism | Angle between geographic north and magnetic north. | Important in navigation; not related to magnetic field strength. |
| Magnetic Inclination (Dip) | Magnetism | Angle between Earth’s magnetic field and horizontal plane. | Distinct from declination; measures tilt of field lines. |
| Ferromagnetism | Magnetism | Strong magnetism due to parallel alignment of spins in domains. | Permanent magnetization possible; differs from paramagnetism. |
| Paramagnetism | Magnetism | Weak attraction due to partial alignment of unpaired spins. | Temporary; disappears when field is removed. |
| Diamagnetism | Magnetism | Weak repulsion due to induced currents opposing applied field. | Universal property; very weak compared to ferro/para. |
| Solenoid | Circuits / Magnetism | A coil of wire that generates a magnetic field when current flows through it. | Produces a nearly uniform magnetic field inside; used in electromagnets and inductors. |
| Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule | Magnetism / Circuits | Rule for direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. | Thumb \= force, First finger \= field, Second finger \= current. Applies to motors. |
| Fleming’s Right-Hand Rule | Magnetism / Circuits | Rule for direction of induced current when a conductor moves in a magnetic field. | Thumb \= motion, First finger \= field, Second finger \= induced current. Applies to generators. |
| Gauss’ Law of Magnetism | Magnetism | One of Maxwell’s equations: the net magnetic flux through a closed surface is zero. | Implies magnetic monopoles do not exist; field lines always form closed loops. |
| Kirchhoff’s Laws | Circuits | Rules for current and voltage in circuits: (1) Current law (sum of currents at junction \= 0), (2) Voltage law (sum of voltages in a loop \= 0). | Essential for analyzing complex circuits. |
| Magnetic Permeability (μ) | Magnetism | Measure of how easily a material supports magnetic field lines. | Analogous to permittivity in electrostatics. |
| Permittivity (ε) | Electrostatics | Measure of how easily a material supports electric field lines. | Analogous to permeability in magnetism. |
| Displacement Current | Electromagnetism | Term added by Maxwell to Ampère’s law to account for changing electric fields. | Key to unifying electricity and magnetism into Maxwell’s equations. |
| Magnetic Hysteresis | Magnetism | Lag between applied field and magnetization in ferromagnets. | Important in permanent magnets and transformers. |
| Magnetic Domains | Magnetism | Regions in ferromagnets where spins align. | Domain walls shift under external fields. |
| Ground (Circuit Ground) | Circuits | Reference point in a circuit, usually 0 volts. | Different from Earth ground (physical connection to Earth). |
| Short Circuit | Circuits | Path of very low resistance causing excessive current. | Dangerous; distinct from open circuit (no current). |
| Open Circuit | Circuits | Break in a circuit preventing current flow. | Opposite of short circuit. |
| Magnetic Declination vs Inclination | Magnetism | Declination \= horizontal angle (north vs magnetic north); Inclination \= vertical tilt of field lines. | Easily confused; one is horizontal, the other vertical. |

**Common Components**

| Component | Description | What It Does | Usage / Application |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Capacitor | A passive component that stores energy in the form of an electric field between two conductive plates separated by an insulator (dielectric). | Holds **charge** and maintains a voltage across its plates temporarily. | Used in timing circuits, filtering signals, smoothing voltage in power supplies, and energy storage. |
| Battery | A device consisting of electrochemical cells that convert chemical energy into electrical energy. | Provides a **steady voltage source** by maintaining potential difference between terminals. | Powers portable devices, backup systems, and serves as DC sources in circuits. |
| Rectifier (Diode Bridge) | An arrangement of diodes that allows current to flow in only one direction. | Converts **AC to DC** by blocking negative half-cycles and allowing positive ones. | Used in power supplies to provide DC output from AC mains. |
| Inverter | An electronic device that uses switching circuits to convert DC into AC. | Converts **DC to AC**, often changing voltage levels as well. | Used in solar power systems, UPS devices, and motor drives. |
| Transformer | A device with two or more coils wound around a magnetic core. | Changes the **ratio of voltage to current** via electromagnetic induction. | Used in power distribution, voltage regulation, and isolation between circuits. |
| Switch | A mechanical or electronic device that opens or closes a circuit path. | Controls whether current flows by making or breaking connections. | Used in everyday appliances, circuit control, and logic systems. |
| Resistor | A passive component that opposes current flow, dissipating energy as heat. | **Reduces current flow** and drops voltage according to Ohm’s law. | Used for current limiting, voltage division, and biasing electronic components. |
| Diode | A semiconductor device that allows current to flow easily in one direction but blocks it in the opposite direction. | Provides **low resistance forward, high resistance reverse**. | Used in rectifiers, signal demodulation, and protection circuits. |
| LED (Light Emitting Diode) | A semiconductor diode that emits light when forward biased. | Converts **electrical energy into light energy**. | Used in indicators, displays, lighting systems, and optical communication. |
| Inductor | A coil of wire that stores energy in a magnetic field when current flows through it. | Opposes changes in current; smooths current flow; can filter signals. | Used in transformers, filters, power supplies, and radio-frequency circuits. |
| Relay | An electromechanical switch operated by an electromagnet. | Allows a low-power signal to control a high-power circuit. | Used in automation, motor control, and protective circuits. |
| Transistor | A semiconductor device with three terminals (base, collector, emitter). | Acts as a switch or amplifier for electrical signals. | Used in digital logic, amplification, and nearly all modern electronics. |
| Fuse | A safety device with a thin wire that melts when current exceeds a limit. | Protects circuits by breaking the connection during overloads. | Used in household wiring, automotive systems, and electronics. |
| Circuit Breaker | A resettable protective device that interrupts current flow during overloads. | Prevents damage by automatically opening the circuit. | Used in electrical panels and industrial systems. |
| Potentiometer (Variable Resistor) | A resistor with an adjustable resistance value. | Allows control of voltage or current levels. | Used in volume controls, tuning circuits, and calibration. |
| Transformer | Two or more coils wound around a magnetic core. | Transfers energy between circuits; changes voltage/current ratios. | Used in power distribution, isolation, and adapters. |
| Rectifier (Diode Bridge) | Arrangement of diodes that converts AC to DC. | Allows current in one direction only. | Used in power supplies. |
| Inverter | Electronic device that converts DC to AC. | Provides AC output from DC sources. | Used in solar systems, UPS, and motor drives. |
| Relay vs Switch | Relay is controlled electrically; switch is controlled mechanically. | Relay enables remote or automated control. | Switches are manual; relays are automatic. |
| SCR (Silicon Controlled Rectifier) | A semiconductor device that acts as a controlled diode. | Allows current only when triggered by a gate signal. | Used in motor speed control, light dimmers, and power regulation. |
| Op-Amp (Operational Amplifier) | High-gain voltage amplifier with differential inputs. | Amplifies voltage differences; can perform math operations. | Used in audio amps, filters, and analog computing. |
| Resonator / Crystal Oscillator | Piezoelectric device that vibrates at a precise frequency. | Provides stable clock signals. | Used in watches, computers, and communication systems. |
| Relay vs Transistor | Relay is electromechanical; transistor is solid-state. | Transistor is faster, smaller, and more durable. | Relays handle high currents; transistors handle logic and amplification. |
| Solenoid | Coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when energized. | Converts electrical energy into linear mechanical motion. | Used in locks, valves, and actuators. |
| LED (Light Emitting Diode) | Diode that emits light when forward biased. | Converts electrical energy into light. | Used in indicators, displays, and lighting. |
| Photodiode | Diode that generates current when exposed to light. | Converts light energy into electrical signals. | Used in sensors, solar cells, and optical communication. |
| Relay vs Contactor | Both are switches operated by electromagnets. | Contactors are designed for high-current loads. | Relays for control circuits; contactors for industrial power circuits. |

## 

## **Wire and connection symbols**

#### **Wire**

Connects components and passes current easily from one part of a circuit to another.

#### **Wires joined**

A 'blob' should be drawn where wires are connected (joined), but it is sometimes omitted. Wires connected at 'crossroads' should be staggered slightly to form two T-junctions, as shown on the right.

#### **Wires not joined**

In complex diagrams it is often necessary to draw wires crossing even though they are not connected. The simple crossing on the left is correct but may be misread as a join where the 'blob' has been forgotten. The bridge symbol on the right leaves no doubt\!

---

## **Power supply symbols**

#### **Cell**

Supplies electrical energy. The larger line is positive (+). A single cell is often called a battery, but strictly speaking a battery is two or more cells joined together.

#### **Battery**

Supplies electrical energy. A battery is more than one cell. The larger line is positive (+).

#### 

#### **Solar Cell**

Converts light to electrical energy.  
The larger line is positive (+).

#### [**DC supply**](https://electronicsclub.info/acdc.htm#dc)

Supplies electrical energy.  
DC \= Direct Current, always flowing in one direction.

#### [**AC supply**](https://electronicsclub.info/acdc.htm#ac)

Supplies electrical energy.  
AC \= Alternating Current, continually changing direction.

#### **Fuse**

A safety device which will 'blow' (melt) if the current flowing through it exceeds a specified value.

#### [**Transformer**](https://electronicsclub.info/powersupplies.htm#transformer)

Two coils of wire linked by an iron core. Transformers are used to step up (increase) and step down (decrease) AC voltages. Energy is transferred between the coils by the magnetic field in the core, there is no electrical connection between the coils.

#### **Earth (Ground)**

A connection to earth. For some electronic circuits this symbol is used for the 0V (zero volts) of the power supply, but for mains electricity and some radio circuits it really means the earth. It is also known as ground.

---

## **Output device symbols**

#### [**Lamp (lighting)**](https://electronicsclub.info/lamps.htm)

A transducer which converts electrical energy to light. This symbol is used for a lamp providing illumination, for example a car headlamp or torch bulb.

#### [**Lamp (indicator)**](https://electronicsclub.info/lamps.htm)

A transducer which converts electrical energy to light. This symbol is used for a lamp which is an indicator, for example a warning light on a car dashboard.

#### **Heater**

A transducer which converts electrical energy to heat.

#### **Motor**

A transducer which converts electrical energy to kinetic energy (motion).

#### **Bell**

A transducer which converts electrical energy to sound.

#### [**Buzzer**](https://electronicsclub.info/other.htm#buzzer)

A transducer which converts electrical energy to sound.

#### [**Inductor, Coil, Solenoid**](https://electronicsclub.info/other.htm#inductor)

A coil of wire which creates a magnetic field when current passes through it. There may be an iron core inside the coil. It can be used as a transducer converting electrical energy to mechanical energy by pulling on something magnetically.

---

## **Switch symbols**

#### [**Push-to-make switch**](https://electronicsclub.info/switches.htm)

A push switch allows current to flow only when the button is pressed. This is the switch used to operate a doorbell.

#### [**Push-to-break switch**](https://electronicsclub.info/switches.htm)

This type of push switch is normally closed \= on, it is open \= off only when the button is pressed.

#### [**SPST, on-off switch**](https://electronicsclub.info/switches.htm)

SPST \= Single Pole, Single Throw. Current flows only when the switch is in the closed \=on position.

#### [**SPDT, 2-way switch**](https://electronicsclub.info/switches.htm)

SPDT \= Single Pole, Double Throw. A 2-way changeover switch directs the flow of current to one of two routes according to its position. Some SPDT switches have a central off position and are described as 'on-off-on'.

#### [**DPST switch**](https://electronicsclub.info/switches.htm)

DPST \= Double Pole, Single Throw. A dual on-off switch which is often used to switch mains electricity because it can isolate both the live and neutral connections.

#### [**DPDT switch**](https://electronicsclub.info/switches.htm)

DPDT \= Double Pole, Double Throw.  
This switch can be wired up as a reversing switch for a motor. Some DPDT switches have a central off position.

#### [**Relay**](https://electronicsclub.info/relays.htm)

An electrically operated switch, for example a 9V battery circuit connected to the coil can switch an AC mains circuit. The rectangle represents the coil.  
NO \= Normally Open, COM \= Common, NC \= Normally  Closed.

---

## **Resistor symbols**

#### [**Resistor**](https://electronicsclub.info/resistors.htm)

A resistor restricts the flow of charge. Uses include limiting the current passing through an LED, and slowly charging a capacitor in a timing circuit.  
Some publications use the old resistor symbol: ![old zig-zag resistor symbol][image32]

#### [**Rheostat variable resistor**](https://electronicsclub.info/variableresistors.htm)

A rheostat has 2 contacts and is usually used to control current. Uses include controlling lamp brightness or motor speed and changing the rate of flow of charge into a capacitor in a timing circuit.

#### [**Potentiometer variable resistor**](https://electronicsclub.info/variableresistors.htm)

A potentiometer has 3 contacts and is usually used to control voltage. It can be used like this as a transducer converting position (angle of the control spindle) to an electrical signal.

#### [**Preset variable resistor**](https://electronicsclub.info/variableresistors.htm)

A preset is operated with a small screwdriver or similar tool. It is designed to be set when the circuit is made and then left without further adjustment. Presets are cheaper than standard variable resistors so they are sometimes used in projects to reduce the cost.

---

## **Capacitor symbols**

#### [**Capacitor, unpolarised**](https://electronicsclub.info/capacitors.htm)

A capacitor stores electric charge. It can be used with a resistor in a timing circuit, for smoothing a supply (it provides a reservoir of charge) and can be used as a filter (blocking DC signals but passing AC signals). Unpolarised capacitors usually have small values, less than 1µF.

#### [**Capacitor, polarised**](https://electronicsclub.info/capacitors.htm)

A capacitor stores electric charge. Polarised capacitors must be connected the correct way round. They usually have larger values, 1µF and greater. See above for uses.

#### [**Variable capacitor**](https://electronicsclub.info/capacitors.htm)

A variable capacitor is used in a radio tuner.

#### [**Trimmer variable capacitor**](https://electronicsclub.info/capacitors.htm)

This type of variable capacitor is designed to be set when a circuit is made and then left without further adjustment.

---

## **Diode symbols**

#### [**Diode**](https://electronicsclub.info/diodes.htm)

A device which allows current to flow in only one direction.

#### [**Light Emitting Diode**](https://electronicsclub.info/leds.htm)

A transducer which converts electrical energy to light. Usually abbreviated to LED.

#### [**Zener diode**](https://electronicsclub.info/diodes.htm#zener)

A zener diode can be used to maintain a fixed voltage.

#### **Photodiode**

A light-sensitive diode.

---

## **Transistor symbols**

#### [**Transistor NPN**](https://electronicsclub.info/transistors.htm)

A transistor amplifies current and can be used with other components to make an amplifier or switching circuit. This symbol is for a bipolar junction transistor (BJT), the type you are most likely to use at first.

#### [**Transistor PNP**](https://electronicsclub.info/transistors.htm)

A transistor amplifies current and can be used with other components to make an amplifier or switching circuit. This symbol is for a bipolar junction transistor (BJT), the type you are most likely to use at first.

#### **Phototransistor**

A light-sensitive transistor.

---

## **Audio and Radio symbols**

#### **Microphone**

A transducer which converts sound to electrical energy.

#### **Earphone**

A transducer which converts electrical energy to sound.

#### [**Loudspeaker**](https://electronicsclub.info/other.htm#loudspeaker)

A transducer which converts electrical energy to sound.

#### [**Piezo Transducer**](https://electronicsclub.info/other.htm#piezo)

A transducer which converts electrical energy to sound.

#### **Amplifier (general symbol)**

An amplifier circuit with one input. Really this is a block diagram symbol because it represents a circuit rather than just one component.

#### **Aerial (Antenna)**

A transmitting device to receive or transmit radio signals, can also act as a receiving device to intercept electromagnetic waves and convert their energy into AC voltage and current. It is also known as an antenna. Creates electromagnetic waves if used with an AC voltage source.

The two open wires of the dipole act as a sort of capacitor (two conductors separated by a dielectric), with the electric field open to dispersal instead of being concentrated between two closely-spaced plates.

The closed wire path of the loop antenna acts like an inductor with a large air core, again providing ample opportunity for the field to disperse away from the antenna instead of being concentrated and contained as in a normal inductor.

As the powered dipole radiates its changing electric field into space, a changing magnetic field is produced at right angles, thus sustaining the electric field further into space, and so on as the wave propagates at the speed of light.

As the powered loop antenna radiates its changing magnetic field into space, a changing electric field is produced at right angles, with the same end-result of a continuous electromagnetic wave sent away from the antenna. Either antenna achieves the same basic task: the controlled production of an electromagnetic field.

---

## **Meters and Oscilloscope**

#### [**Voltmeter**](https://electronicsclub.info/meters.htm#voltmeters)

Measures voltage. The proper name for voltage is 'potential difference' but voltage is more widely used.

#### [**Ammeter**](https://electronicsclub.info/meters.htm#ammeters)

Measures current.

#### 

#### [**Galvanometer**](https://electronicsclub.info/meters.htm#galvanometers)

A very sensitive meter used to measure tiny currents, usually 1mA or less.

#### [**Ohmmeter**](https://electronicsclub.info/meters.htm#ohmmeters)

Measures resistance. Most multimeters have an ohmmeter setting.

#### [**Oscilloscope**](https://electronicsclub.info/cro.htm)

An oscilloscope is used to display the 'shape' of electrical signals \- showing how they vary with time. It can be used to measure voltage and time periods.

---

## **Sensors (input devices)**

#### [**LDR**](https://electronicsclub.info/other.htm#ldr)

A transducer which converts brightness (light) to resistance (an electrical property). LDR \= Light Dependent Resistor

#### [**Thermistor**](https://electronicsclub.info/other.htm#thermistor)

A transducer which converts temperature (heat) to resistance (an electrical property).

**Electric Field**  
$F=\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{\left|{q}\right|\left|{{q}_{0}}\right|}{{r}^{2}}\ (Coulomb's\ Law)$  
$E=\frac{F}{{q}_{0}}=\ \frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{\left|{q}\right|}{{r}^{2}}\ (point\ charge)$

$E=\frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}{z}^{2}}[(1-\frac{d}{2z}{)}^{-2}-(1+\frac{d}{2z}{)}^{-2}]$  
$binomial\ theorem\ expansion:$  
$[(1-\frac{d}{2z}{)}^{-2}-(1+\frac{d}{2z}{)}^{-2}]\ =\ [(1+\frac{2d}{2z(1!)}+...)-(1-\frac{2d}{2z(1!)}+...)]$  
$E\ =\ \frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}{z}^{2}}[(1+\frac{d}{z}+...)-(1-\frac{d}{z}+...)]$  
$since\ \frac{d}{z}\ll 1$  
$E=\frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{2d}{z}=\frac{1}{2\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{qd}{{z}^{3}}=\frac{1}{2\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{p}{{z}^{3}}\ (electric\ dipole)$  
$\vec{p}=electric\ dipole\ moment=q\vec{d}$

**Electric Field of Charged Rings**

$E=\frac{qz}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}({z}^{2}+{R}^{2}{)}^{\frac{3}{2}}}\ （charged\ ring)$

**Electric Field of Charged Disks & Infinite Sheets**  
![][image116]![][image117]![][image118]![][image119]  
$E=\frac{\sigma }{2{\epsilon }_{0}}(1-\frac{z}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+{R}^{2}}})\ (charged\ disk)$  
$\lim\limits_{{R} \rightarrow {\infty }}E=\frac{\sigma }{2{\epsilon }_{0}}\ (infinite\ sheet)$  
$if\ z\gg R,\ far\ from\ the\ disk$  
$binomial\ theorem\ expansion:$  
$\frac{z}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+{R}^{2}}}=\frac{z}{z\sqrt{1+\frac{{R}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}}}=(1+\frac{{R}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}{)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}$  
$(1+\frac{{R}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}{)}^{-\frac{1}{2}}=1+\frac{-\frac{1}{2}}{1!}\frac{{R}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}+\frac{-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}-1)}{2!}\frac{{R}^{4}}{{z}^{4}}+...$  
$\frac{z}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+{R}^{2}}}=1-\frac{{R}^{2}}{2{z}^{2}}$		$E=\frac{\sigma }{2{\epsilon }_{0}}[1-(1-\frac{{R}^{2}}{2{z}^{2}})]=\frac{\sigma }{4{\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{{R}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}$  
$for\ the\ disk:\ \sigma =\frac{q}{A},\ A=\pi {R}^{2},\ then:$  
$E=\frac{\sigma }{4{\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{{R}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}=\frac{q}{4{\epsilon }_{0}\pi {R}^{2}}\frac{{R}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{q}{{z}^{2}}\ (point\ on\ central\ axis\ where\ z\gg R,\ same\ as\ particle)$

When the electric field in a material is large enough, the material undergoes ***electrical breakdown*** in which conducting paths suddenly appear in the material. Electrical breakdown occurs in air (at atmospheric pressure) when the electric field exceeds about 3 x 106 N/C. During breakdown, electrons flow along one or more conducting paths, creating ***electric sparks***.

![][image120]![][image121]  
    $\tau =p\times E\ (torque\ on\ a\ dipole)$
