**Gauss’ Law & Gaussian Surfaces**  
$\Phi =\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}\ (electric\ flux\ through\ a\ Gaussian\ surface)$  
${\epsilon }_{0}\Phi ={\epsilon }_{0}\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}={q}_{enc}\ (Gauss'\ Law)$

**Electric Field of Conducting Surfaces**  
$(Gaussian\ surface\ small\ enough,\ ununiform\ E\ treated\ as\ uniform)$  
${\epsilon }_{0}EA={q}_{enc}=\sigma A$  
$E=\frac{\sigma }{{\epsilon }_{0}}\ (conducting\ surface)$  
Magnitude of the electric field at a location just outside a conductor is proportional to the surface charge density at that location on the conductor

**Electric Field of Straight Line of Charge**  
$\Phi =EAcos\theta =E(2\pi rh)$  
${\epsilon }_{0}\Phi ={q}_{enc}$  
${\epsilon }_{0}E(2\pi rh)=\lambda h$  
$E=\frac{\lambda }{2\pi {\epsilon }_{0}r}\ (infinitely\ long\ straight\ line\ of\ charge)$  
**Electric Field of Nonconducting Sheets**  
Thin, infinite, nonconducting sheet with a uniform (positive) surface charge density $\sigma$.  
${\epsilon }_{0}(EA+EA)=\sigma A$  
$E=\frac{\sigma }{2{\epsilon }_{0}}\ (sheet\ of\ charge)$

**Electric Field of Pair of Conducting Plates**  
Thin, infinite, conducting plates with excess positive and negative charges, each with a uniform surface charge density of magnitude ${\sigma }_{1}$.  
$E=\frac{{\sigma }_{1}}{{\epsilon }_{0}}\ (just\ outside\ of\ the\ individual\ plates)$  
When brought together, excess charge on one plate attracts that on the other, and all the excess charge moves onto the inner faces of the plates. The new surface density is now twice ${\sigma }_{1}$.  
$E=\frac{2{\sigma }_{1}}{{\epsilon }_{0}}=\frac{\sigma }{{\epsilon }_{0}}\ (pair\ of\ conducting\ plates)$

**Voltage (Electric Potential)**  
${V}_{f}-{V}_{i}=-\int\limits_{i}^{f}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}$  		$if\ set\ i=\infty ,\ then\ {V}_{i}=0,\ V=-\int\limits_{i}^{f}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}$  
**Electric Potential of Dipoles**  
$V=\frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{{r}_{(-)}-{r}_{(+)}}{{r}_{(-)}{r}_{(+)}}$  
$when\ r\gg d,\ {r}_{(-)}-{r}_{(+)}\approx dcos\theta ,\ {r}_{(-)}{r}_{(+)}\approx {r}^{2}$  
$V=\frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{dcos\theta }{{r}^{2}}$  
$V=\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{pcos\theta }{{r}^{2}}\ (electric\ dipole)$

**Induced Dipole Moments**  
Many molecules, such as water, have permanent electric dipole moments. In other molecules (called nonpolar molecules) and in every isolated atom, the centers of the positive and negative charges coincide (Fig. a) and thus no dipole moment is set up. However, if we place an atom or a nonpolar molecule in an external electric field, the field distorts the electron orbits and separates the centers of positive and negative charge (Fig. b). Because the electrons are negatively charged, they tend to be shifted in a direction opposite the field.This shift sets up a dipole moment that points in the direction of the field. This dipole moment is said to be induced by the field, and the atom or molecule is then said to be polarized by the field (that is, it has a positive side and a negative side).When the field is removed, the induced dipole moment and the polarization disappear.

**Electric Potential of Charged Rods**  
$V=\int\limits_{}^{}dV=\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\int\limits_{}^{}\frac{dq}{r}$  
$for\ a\ line\ of\ charge,\ dq=\lambda dx,\ r=({x}^{2}+{d}^{2}{)}^{\frac{1}{2}}$  
$V=\int\limits_{}^{}dV=\int\limits_{0}^{L}\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{\lambda }{({x}^{2}+{d}^{2}{)}^{\frac{1}{2}}}dx$  
$V=\frac{\lambda }{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}ln[\frac{L+({L}^{2}+{d}^{2}{)}^{\frac{1}{2}}}{d}]$

**Electric Potential of Charged Disks**  
$for\ a\ charged\ disk,\ dq=\sigma (2\pi R')(dR')$  
$dV=\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{dq}{r}=\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{\sigma (2\pi R')(dR')}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+R{'}^{2}}}$  
$V=\int\limits_{}^{}dV=\frac{\sigma }{2{\epsilon }_{0}}\int\limits_{0}^{R}\frac{R'dR'}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+R{'}^{2}}}=\frac{\sigma }{2{\epsilon }_{0}}(\sqrt{{z}^{2}+{R}^{2}}-z)$

**Calculating Electric Field From Potential**  
$-{q}_{0}dV={q}_{0}Ecos\theta ds$  
$Ecos\theta =-\frac{dV}{ds}$  
${E}_{s}=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial s}$  
Partial derivative emphasizes that the equation involves only the variation of V along a specified axis (here called the s axis) and only the component of E along that axis.

**Capacitors**  
$q=C{V}_{0}(1-{e}^{-t/RC})\ (charging\ capacitor)$  
$i=\frac{dq}{dt}=\frac{{V}_{0}}{R}{e}^{-t/RC}\ (charging\ capacitor)$  
${V}_{c}=\frac{q}{C}={V}_{0}(1-{e}^{-t/RC})\ (charging\ capacitor)$  
$\tau =RC\ (capacitive\ time\ constant)$  
$q={q}_{0}{e}^{-t/RC}\ (discharging\ capacitor)$  
$i=\frac{dq}{dt}=-\frac{{q}_{0}}{RC}{e}^{-t/RC}\ (discharging\ capacitor)$  
${V}_{c}={V}_{0}({e}^{-t/RC})\ (discharging\ capacitor)$

**Parallel Plate Capacitors**  
$q=CV$  
$Gauss'\ Law\ reduces\ when\ \vec{E}\ is\ constant\ and\ parallel\ to\ d\vec{A}$  
$q={\epsilon }_{0}EA$  
${V}_{f}-{V}_{i}=-\int\limits_{i}^{f}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}$  
Always choose a path that follows an electric field line from the positive plate to the negative plate (the image on the left is in the opposite direction)  
$V=\int\limits_{+}^{-}Eds$  
$V=\int\limits_{+}^{-}Eds=E\int\limits_{0}^{d}ds=Ed$  
$C=\frac{{\epsilon }_{0}A}{d}\ (parallel\ plate\ capacitor)$  
$for\ capacitance\ calculation\ simplicity:\ {\epsilon }_{0}=8.85\times 1{0}^{-12}{C}^{2}/N\cdot {m}^{2}=8.85\times 1{0}^{-12}F/m=8.85pF/m$

**Cylindrical Capacitors (Coaxial/Cylindrical Shell)**  
For a cylindrical capacitor of length $L$ formed by two coaxial cylinders of radii a and b, we assume that $L\gg b$ so that we can neglect the fringing of the electric field at the ends.  
$q={\epsilon }_{0}EA={\epsilon }_{0}E(2\pi rL)$  
$E=\frac{q}{2\pi {\epsilon }_{0}Lr}$  
$V=\int\limits_{+}^{-}Eds=\frac{q}{2\pi {\epsilon }_{0}L}\int\limits_{a}^{b}\frac{dr}{r}=\frac{q}{2\pi {\epsilon }_{0}L}ln(\frac{b}{a})$  
$C=2\pi {\epsilon }_{0}\frac{L}{ln(b/a)}\ (cylindrical\ capacitor)$

**Spherical Capacitors**  
The image to the right can also serve as a central cross section of a capacitor that consists of two concentric spherical shells, of radii a and b.  
$q={\epsilon }_{0}EA={\epsilon }_{0}E(4\pi {r}^{2})$		$E=\frac{1}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{q}{{r}^{2}}$ $V=\int\limits_{+}^{-}Eds=\frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\int\limits_{a}^{b}\frac{dr}{{r}^{2}}=\frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b})=\frac{q}{4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}}\frac{b-a}{ab}$  
$C=4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}\frac{ab}{b-a}\ (spherical\ capacitor)$

**Single Isolated Spherical Conductors**  
We can assign a capacitance to a ***single isolated spherical conductor*** of radius R by assuming that the “missing plate” is a conducting sphere of infinite radius.  
$C=4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}\frac{ab}{b-a}=4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}\frac{a}{1-a/b}$  
$as\ b\rightarrow \infty \ and\ substitute\ R\ for\ a:\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ C=4\pi {\epsilon }_{0}R\ (isolated\ sphere)$

**Capacitor Potential Energy**  
$dW=V'dq'=\frac{q'}{C}dq',\ where\ V',q'=voltage\ and\ charge\ at\ instant\ of\ charging$  
$W=\int\limits_{}^{}dW=\frac{1}{C}\int\limits_{0}^{q}q'dq'=\frac{{q}^{2}}{2C}$ 			$U=\frac{{q}^{2}}{2C}=\frac{1}{2}C{V}^{2}\ (potential\ energy)$

**Capacitor Energy Density of Electric Field**  
${u}_{E}=\frac{U}{Ad}=\frac{C{V}^{2}}{2Ad}$	$C=\frac{{\epsilon }_{0}A}{d}$	${u}_{E}=\frac{1}{2}{\epsilon }_{0}(\frac{V}{d}{)}^{2}$	$\frac{V}{d}=E$ 	${u}_{E}=\frac{1}{2}{\epsilon }_{0}{E}^{2}$  
${u}_{E}=energy\ density,\ d=distance\ separation\ between\ capacitors$

**Capacitance with Dielectric Material**  
Dielectric material increases capacitance by the dielectric constant, limiting the potential difference that can be applied between the plates to a certain value Vmax, called the ***breakdown potential***. If this value is substantially exceeded, the dielectric material will break down and form a conducting path between the plates. Every dielectric material has characteristic ***dielectric strength***, which is the maximum value of the electric field that it can tolerate without breakdown.  
$C={\epsilon }_{0}ℒ$	$ℒ=\frac{(effective\ area\ collecting\ charge)}{(effective\ distance\ for\ fields)}=geometry\ factor\ with\ units\ of\ length$  
$C=\kappa {\epsilon }_{0}ℒ=\kappa {C}_{air}$		${C}_{air}=capacitance\ with\ only\ air\ between\ plates$  
In a region completely filled by a dielectric material of dielectric constant $\kappa$, all electrostatic equations containing the permittivity constant ${\epsilon }_{0}$ are to be modified by replacing ${\epsilon }_{0}$ with $\kappa {\epsilon }_{0}$. 

*For a **fixed distribution of charges**, the effect of a dielectric is to **decrease the electric field, the electric potential difference, and decrease the potential energy.***  
*For a **fixed potential difference**, the effect of a dielectric is to **increase charge stored, increase potential energy, while the electric field remains constant.***

1. **Polar dielectrics:** the electric dipoles tend to line up with an external electric field. Because the molecules are continuously jostling each other as a result of their random thermal motion, this alignment is not complete, but it becomes more complete as the magnitude of the applied field is increased (or as the temperature, and thus the jostling, is decreased). The alignment of the electric dipoles produces an electric field that is opposite the applied field and smaller in magnitude than that field.  
2. **Nonpolar dielectrics:** molecules acquire dipole moments by induction when placed in an external electric field. This external field tends to “stretch” the molecule, separating slightly the centers of negative and positive charge. 

${\epsilon }_{0}\oint\limits_{}^{}\kappa \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}=q\ (Gauss'\ law\ with\ dielectric)$  
$\vec{D}={\epsilon }_{0}\kappa \vec{E}=electric\ displacement$		$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{D}\cdot d\vec{A}=q$  
The charge q enclosed by the Gaussian surface is now taken to be the ***free charge only***. The induced surface charge on the dielectric is deliberately ignored on the right side of this equation, having been taken fully into account by introducing the dielectric constant $\kappa$ on the left side.

The simple electrostatic apparatus used by Faraday. An assembled apparatus (second from left) forms a spherical capacitor consisting of a central brass ball and a concentric brass shell. Faraday placed dielectric materials in the space between the ball and the shell.

**Currents**  
$i=\frac{dq}{dt}\ (definition\ of\ current)$		$q=\int\limits_{}^{}dq=\int\limits_{0}^{t}idt$  
$i=\int\limits_{}^{}\vec{J}\cdot d\vec{A}$		$J=current\ density$	  
Assuming current is uniform across the surface and parallel to $d\vec{A}$, then $J$ is also uniform and parallel to $d\vec{A}$.  
$i=\int\limits_{}^{}Jda=J\int\limits_{}^{}dA=JA$		$J=\frac{i}{A}$  
*$J$ has the same direction as the field, magnitude equal current per unit area through the element of that surface.*

$q=(nAL)e$		$n=number\ of\ charge\ carriers\ per\ unit\ volume$  
$t=\frac{L}{{v}_{d}}$	${v}_{d}=electron\ drift\ speed$  
$i=\frac{q}{t}=\frac{nALe}{L/{v}_{d}}=nAe{v}_{d}$  
${v}_{d}=\frac{i}{nAe}=\frac{J}{ne}$  
$\vec{J}=(ne)\vec{{v}_{d}}$		$ne=carrier\ charge\ density$

**Resistance**  
$R=\frac{V}{i}\ (definition\ of\ resistance\ R)$  
$\rho =\frac{E}{J}\ (definition\ of\ resistivity\ \rho )$ 	$unit\ (\rho )=\frac{unit\ (E)}{unit\ (J)}=\frac{V/m}{A/{m}^{2}}=\frac{V}{A}m=\Omega \cdot m$  
$thus,\ \vec{E}=\rho \vec{J}$ 	these two resistivity equations only hold for ***isotropic material***—materials whose electrical properties are the same in all directions  
$\sigma =\frac{1}{\rho }\ (definition\ of\ conductivity\ \sigma )$  
$\vec{J}=\sigma \vec{E}$  
Resistance is a property of an object. Resistivity is a property of a material.  
*$E=\frac{V}{L}$ 	$J=\frac{i}{A}$	$\rho =\frac{E}{J}=\frac{V/L}{i/A}$	$R=\rho \frac{L}{A}$*  
**Variation with Temperature**  
$\rho -{\rho }_{0}={\rho }_{0}\alpha (T-{T}_{0})$	$\alpha =temperature\ coefficient$	  
${T}_{0}=reference\ temperature,\ {\rho }_{0}=resistivity\ at\ that\ temperature$  
Usually, ${T}_{0}=293K\ (room\ temp)$

**Ohm’s Law**  
A conducting material obeys Ohm’s law when the resistivity of the material is independent of the magnitude and direction of the applied electric field.

The motion of the electrons in an electric field E is a combination of the motion due to random collisions and that due to E. When we consider all the free electrons, their random motions average to zero and make no contribution to the drift speed. Thus the drift speed is due only to the effect of the electric field on the electrons.

If an electron of mass m is placed in an electric field of magnitude E, the electron will experience an acceleration $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{eE}{m}$. 

The nature of the collisions experienced by electrons is such that, after a typical collision, the electron will—so to speak—completely lose its memory of its previous drift velocity. Each electron will then start off fresh after every encounter, moving off in a random direction. In the average time $\tau$ between collision, the average electron will acquire a drift speed of ${v}_{d}=a\tau$. Moreover, if we measure the drift speeds of all the electrons at any instant, we will find that their average drift speed is also $a\tau$. thus, at any instant, on average, the electrons will have drift speed ${v}_{d}=a\tau$.

${v}_{d}=a\tau =\frac{eE\tau }{m}=\frac{J}{ne}$	$E=(\frac{m}{{e}^{2}n\tau })J$		$\rho =\frac{m}{{e}^{2}n\tau }$	

$J=current\ density$	$\rho =resistivity$

**Power**  
$dU=dqV=idtV$  
$P=iV\ (rate\ of\ electrical\ energy\ transfer)$  
$P={i}^{2}R\ (resistive\ dissipation)$  
$P=\frac{{V}^{2}}{R}\ (resistive\ dissipation)$  
The resistive dissipation power equations only apply to the transfer of electric potential energy to thermal energy in a resistance, while the first one applies to electrical energy transfers of all kinds.

**Circuits**  
$\epsilon =\frac{dW}{dq}\ (definition\ of\ \epsilon )$	$\epsilon =EMF=electromotive\ force$

* **Ideal emf device:** lacks any internal resistance to the internal movement of charge from terminal to terminal. The potential difference between the terminals of an ideal emf device is equal to the emf of the device.   
* **Real emf device:** has internal resistance to the internal movement of charge. When a real emf device is not connected to a circuit, and thus does not have current through it, the potential difference between its terminals is equal to its emf. However, when that device has current through it, the potential difference between its terminals differs from its emf.

**Magnetic Fields**  
$B=\frac{{F}_{B}}{|q|v}$  
$\vec{{F}_{B}}=q\vec{v}\times \vec{B}$  
${F}_{B}=|q|vBsin\phi$

**Geomagnetic south pole:** acts as the north pole of a bar magnet. Arctic direction, the typical north.  
**Geomagnetic north pole:** acts as the south pole of a bar magnet. Antarctic direction, the typical south.

**Hall Effect**  
a copper strip of width d, carrying a current i whose conventional direction is from the top of the figure to the bottom. The charge carriers are electrons and, as we know, they drift (with drift speed vd) in the opposite direction, from bottom to top. At the instant shown in Fig. 28-8a, an external magnetic field $\vec{B}$, pointing into the plane of the figure, has just been turned on. From Eq. $i=\frac{\epsilon }{R}$ we see that a magnetic deflecting force $\vec{{F}_{B}}$will act on each drifting electron, pushing it toward the right edge of the strip. 

As time goes on, electrons move to the right, mostly piling up on the right edge of the strip, leaving uncompensated positive charges in fixed positions at the left edge.The separation of positive charges on the left edge and negative charges on the right edge produces an electric field $\vec{E}$ within the strip, pointing from left to right in Fig. 28-8b. This field exerts an electric force on each electron, tending to push it to the left. Thus, this electric force $\vec{{F}_{E}}$on the electrons, which opposes the magnetic force on them, begins to build up. 

***Equilibrium.*** An equilibrium quickly develops in which the electric force on each electron has increased enough to match the magnetic force. When this happens, as Fig. (b) shows, the force due to $\vec{B}$ and the force due to $\vec{E}$ are in balance. The drifting electrons then move along the strip toward the top of the page at velocity $\vec{{v}_{d}}$with no further collection of electrons on the right edge of the strip and thus no further increase in the electric field $\vec{E}$. 

A ***Hall potential difference V*** is associated with the electric field across strip width d. The magnitude of that potential difference is $V=Ed$. By connecting a voltmeter across the width, we can measure the potential difference between the two edges of the strip. Moreover, the voltmeter can tell us which edge is at higher potential. For the situation of Fig. (b), we would find that the left edge is at higher potential, which is consistent with our assumption that the charge carriers are negatively charged.

***Number Density.*** When the electric and magnetic forces are in balance:  
$eE=e{v}_{d}B$  
${v}_{d}=\frac{J}{ne}=\frac{i}{neA}$  
$n=\frac{Bi}{Vle}$

***Drift Speed.*** The metal strip is moved mechanically through the magnetic field in a direction opposite that of the drift velocity of the charge carriers. The speed of the moving strip is then adjusted until the Hall potential difference vanishes. At this condition, with no Hall effect, the velocity of the charge carriers *with respect to the laboratory frame must be zero*, so the velocity of the strip must be equal in magnitude but opposite the direction of the velocity of the negative charge carriers.

***Electric Potential.*** 		$V=vBd$

**A Circulating Charged Particle**  
**$qvB=\frac{m{v}^{2}}{r}$**  
**$r=\frac{mv}{qB}\ (radius\ of\ circulation)$**  
**$T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi }{v}\frac{mv}{qB}=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}\ (period)$**  
**$f=\frac{1}{T}=\frac{qB}{2\pi m}\ (frequency)$**  
**$\omega =2\pi f=\frac{qB}{m}\ (angular\ frequency)$**

**Helical Path**  
${v}_{||}=vcos\phi$		${v}_{\bot }=vsin\phi$  
$p={v}_{||}T=vcos\phi \frac{2\pi m}{qB}\ (pitch)$  
The parallel component determines the ***pitch p*** of the helix—that is, the distance between adjacent turns (Fig. b). The perpendicular component determines the radius of the helix and is the quantity to be substituted for v in Eq. $r=\frac{mv}{qB}$.

Fig. (c) shows a charged particle spiraling in a nonuniform magnetic field. The more closely spaced field lines at the left and right sides indicate that the magnetic field is stronger there.When the field at an end is strong enough, the particle “reflects” from that end. If the particle reflects from both ends, it is said to be trapped in a ***magnetic bottle***.

**Cyclotrons and Synchrotrons**  
The two hollow D-shaped objects (open on their straight edges) are made of sheet copper. These dees, as they are called, form part of an electrical oscillator, which establishes an alternating potential difference across the gap between them. The dees are immersed in a magnetic field (B=1.5T) whose direction is out of the plane of the page and which is set up by a large electromagnet.

The proton circulation frequency must match the fixed frequency of the electric oscillator.  
$f={f}_{osc}\ (resonance\ condition)$   
$qB=2\pi m{f}_{osc}$  
Conventional cyclotron fails above 50MeV due to its decrease in speed relativistically; the magnet would also become increasingly expensive. → ***proton synchrotron.***  
Field B and oscillator frequency fosc are made to vary with time during the accelerating cycle.  
The proton synchrotron at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Illinois has a circumference 6.3km and can produce protons with energies of about 1 TeV (=1012eV).

**Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Wire**  
$q=it=i\frac{L}{{v}_{d}}$  
${F}_{B}=q{v}_{d}Bsin\phi =\frac{iL}{{v}_{d}}{v}_{d}Bsin90°=iLB$	$\phi$\=angle current and B  
$\vec{{F}_{B}}=i\vec{L}\times \vec{B}\ (force\ on\ a\ current)$  
$if\ wire\ is\ not\ straight:$  
$d\vec{{F}_{B}}=id\vec{L}\times \vec{B}$

**Torque on a Current Loop**

Rectangle length a width b  
${F}_{2}=ibBsin(90°-\theta )=ibBcos\theta ={-F}_{4}\ (see\ Fig.\ 2\ above)$  
${F}_{1}=iaBcos\theta =-{F}_{3}\ but\ different\ axis$  
$\tau '=(iaB\frac{b}{2}sin\theta )+(iaB\frac{b}{2}sin\theta )=iabsin\theta \ (single\ loop)$  
$\tau =N\tau '=NiabBsin\theta =(NiA)Bsin\theta$	    $A=ab=Area$	   $N=#\ of\ turns\ of\ coil$  
A current-carrying flat coil placed in a magnetic field will tend to rotate so that the plane normal vector n points in the field direction.

**Magnetic Dipole**  
The current-carrying coil could be described with a single vector μ, its **magnetic dipole moment**. Direction of μ \= direction of normal vector n.  
$\mu =NiA\ (magnetic\ moment)$  
$\tau =\mu Bsin\theta$		$\theta =angle\ between\ \vec{\mu }\ and\ \vec{B}$  
$\vec{\tau }=\vec{\mu }\times \vec{B}$		$similar\ to\ electric\ dipole\ \vec{\tau }=\vec{p}\times \vec{E}$  
$U(\theta )=-\vec{\mu }\cdot \vec{B}\ (magnetic\ potential\ energy\ that\ change\ the\ orientation\ of\ dipole)$

A magnetic dipole has its lowest energy when its dipole moment is lined up with the magnetic field; it has its highest energy when the dipole moment is in direction opposite the field.

The difference in energy between these two orientations is:  
$\Delta U=(+\mu B)-(-\mu B)=2\mu B$  
This much work must be done by an external agent to turn a magnetic dipole through 180°, starting when the dipole is lined up with the magnetic field.

**Magnetic Field due to a Current**  
$dB=\frac{{\mu }_{0}}{4\pi }\frac{i\ ds\ sin\theta }{{r}^{2}}$  
${\mu }_{0}=4\pi \times 1{0}^{-7}\approx 1.26\times 1{0}^{-6}\ T\cdot m/A\ (permeability\ constant)$  
$d\vec{B}=\frac{{\mu }_{0}}{4\pi }\frac{i\ d\vec{s}\times \vec{r}}{{r}^{3}}\ (Biot-Savart\ law)$

**Magnetic Field due to Long Straight Wires**  
$B=2\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }dB=\frac{{\mu }_{0}i}{2\pi }\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\frac{sin\theta \ ds}{{r}^{2}}$  
$r=\sqrt{{s}^{2}+{R}^{2}}$	$sin\theta =sin(\pi -\theta )=\frac{R}{\sqrt{{s}^{2}+{R}^{2}}}$  
$B=\frac{{\mu }_{0}i}{2\pi }\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\frac{R\ ds}{({s}^{2}+{R}^{2}{)}^{3/2}}=\frac{{\mu }_{0}i}{2\pi R}$  
$B=\frac{{\mu }_{0}i}{2\pi r}\ (long\ straight\ wire)$

**Magnetic Field due to Circular Arc**  
$B=\int\limits_{}^{}dB=\int\limits_{0}^{\phi }\frac{{\mu }_{0}}{4\pi }\frac{iR\ d\phi }{{R}^{2}}=\frac{{\mu }_{0}i}{4\pi R}\int\limits_{0}^{\phi }d\phi$  
$B=\frac{{\mu }_{0}i\phi }{4\pi R}\ (at\ center\ of\ circular\ arc)$	$\phi$ must be in radians

**Parallel Currents**  
${B}_{a}=\frac{{\mu }_{0}{i}_{a}}{2\pi d}$	$\vec{{F}_{ba}}={i}_{b}\vec{L}\times {\vec{B}}_{a}$ (force on b by wire a)  
${F}_{ba}={i}_{b}L{B}_{a}sin90°=\frac{{\mu }_{0}L{i}_{a}{i}_{b}}{2\pi d}$  
Parallel currents attract, antiparallel currents repel  
The force acting between currents in parallel wires is the basis for the ***definition of the ampere***. The definition, adopted in 1946, is this: The ampere is that constant current which, if maintained in two straight, parallel conductors of infinite length, of negligible circular cross section, and placed 1 m apart in vacuum, would produce on each of these conductors a force of 2 x 10\-7 newton per meter of length.

**Ampere’s Law**  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{s}={\mu }_{0}{i}_{enc}\ (Ampere's\ law)$  
integrated over an Amperian loop.

**Magnetic Field Inside a Long Straight Wire**  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{s}=B\oint\limits_{}^{}ds=B2\pi r$  
${i}_{enc}=i\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{\pi {R}^{2}}$		$B2\pi r={\mu }_{0}i\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{\pi {R}^{2}}$  
$B=(\frac{{\mu }_{0}i}{2\pi {R}^{2}})r$

**Magnetic Field of an Ideal Solenoid**  
${i}_{enc}=i(nh)$  
$B={\mu }_{0}in\ (ideal\ solenoid)$	$n=#\ of\ turns$

**Magnetic Field of a Toroid**  
$(B)(2\pi r)={\mu }_{0}iN$  
$B=\frac{{\mu }_{0}iN}{2\pi }\frac{1}{r}\ (toroid)$

**Magnetic Field of a Coil**  
$B(z)=\frac{{\mu }_{0}i{R}^{2}}{2({R}^{2}+{z}^{2}{)}^{3/2}}$  
$when\ z\gg R,\ B(z)\approx \frac{{\mu }_{0}i{R}^{2}}{2{z}^{3}}$  
$\vec{B}(z)=\frac{{\mu }_{0}}{2\pi }\frac{\vec{\mu }}{{z}^{3}}\ (current-carrying\ coil)$

**Faraday’s Law**  
$\epsilon =-\frac{d{\Phi }_{B}}{dt}\ (Faraday's\ law)$  
$\epsilon =-N\frac{d{\Phi }_{B}}{dt}\ (coil\ of\ N\ turns)$  
$P=Fv$  
$\Phi =BA=BLx$  
$\epsilon =\frac{d\Phi }{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}BLx=BL\frac{dx}{dt}=BLv$  
$i=\frac{BLv}{R}$  
${\vec{F}}_{d}=i\vec{L}\times \vec{B}$  
$F=\frac{{B}^{2}{L}^{2}v}{R}$  
$P=Fv=\frac{{B}^{2}{L}^{2}{v}^{2}}{R}$

**Reformulation of Faraday’s Law**  
$\int\limits_{}^{}\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s}=({q}_{0}E)(2\pi r)$  
$\epsilon =2\pi rE$  
$W=\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s}={q}_{0}\oint\limits_{}^{}E\cdot d\vec{s}$  
$\epsilon =\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}$  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}=-\frac{d{\Phi }_{B}}{dt}\ (Faraday's\ law)$  
Electric potential has meaning only for electric fields that are produced by static charges; it has no meaning for electric fields that are produced by induction.  
It starts and ends at the same point, having different electric potentials at the same point is impossible.  
When magnetic flux present, potential \= \-d𝚽B/dt

**Inductors and Inductance**  
$L=\frac{N\Phi }{i}\ (inductance\ defined)$  
Inductors are typically solenoids, N \= \# of turns, N𝚽 \= magnetic flux linkage  
$B={\mu }_{0}in$  
$L=\frac{N\Phi }{i}=\frac{(nl)(BA)}{i}=\frac{(nl)({\mu }_{0}in)(A)}{i}$	n=\# of turns per unit length  
$\frac{L}{l}={\mu }_{0}{n}^{2}A\ (solenoid)$	inductance per unit length

**Self-Induction**  
Self-inductance is the property of a single coil where a change in its own current creates a changing magnetic flux through itself, inducing an emf that opposes that change (Lenz’s law).  
$N\Phi =Li$  
${\epsilon }_{L}=-\frac{d(N\Phi )}{dt}$  
${\epsilon }_{L}=-L\frac{di}{dt}\ (self-induced\ emf)$  
Direction is found using Lenz’ law, this increase in the current is the “change” that the self-induction must oppose. For such opposition to occur, a self-induced emf must appear in the coil, pointing so as to oppose the increase in the current.

**RL Circuits**  
Initially, an inductor acts to oppose changes in the current through it. A long time later, it acts like ordinary connecting wire.  
$-iR-L\frac{di}{dt}+\epsilon =0$  
$L\frac{di}{dt}+Ri=\epsilon \ (RL\ circuit)$  
$i=\frac{\epsilon }{R}(1-{e}^{-Rt/L})\ (rise\ of\ current)$  
${\tau }_{L}=\frac{L}{R}\ (inductive\ time\ constant)$  
$i=\frac{\epsilon }{R}{e}^{-t/{\tau }_{L}}={i}_{0}{e}^{-t/{\tau }_{L}}\ (decay\ of\ current)$

**Energy Stored in a Magnetic Field**  
$\epsilon i=Li\frac{di}{dt}+{i}^{2}R$  
$\frac{d{U}_{B}}{dt}=Li\frac{di}{dt}$  
$d{U}_{B}=Li\ di$  
$\int\limits_{0}^{{U}_{B}}d{U}_{B}=\int\limits_{0}^{i}Li\ di$  
${U}_{B}=\frac{1}{2}L{i}^{2}\ (magnetic\ energy)$  
**Energy Density of a Magnetic Field**  
${\mu }_{B}=\frac{{U}_{B}}{Al}$  
${\mu }_{B}=\frac{L{i}^{2}}{2Al}=\frac{L}{l}\frac{{i}^{2}}{2A}=\frac{1}{2}{\mu }_{0}{n}^{2}{i}^{2}$		${\mu }_{B}=\frac{{B}^{2}}{2{\mu }_{0}}\ (magnetic\ energy\ density)$

**Mutual Induction**  
Mutual inductance is the property of two nearby coils where a changing current in one coil creates a changing magnetic flux in the other coil, inducing an emf in the second coil.

${M}_{2\ 1}=\frac{{N}_{2}{\Phi }_{2\ 1}}{{i}_{1}}$	mutual inductance of coil 2 with respect to coil 1  
${M}_{2\ 1}{i}_{1}={N}_{2}{\Phi }_{2\ 1}$  
${M}_{2\ 1}\frac{d{i}_{1}}{dt}={N}_{2}\frac{d{\Phi }_{2\ 1}}{dt}$  
${\epsilon }_{2}=-{M}_{2\ 1}\frac{d{i}_{1}}{dt}$  
${\epsilon }_{1}=-{M}_{1\ 2}\frac{d{i}_{2}}{dt}$  
${M}_{2\ 1}={M}_{1\ 2}=M$

**Gauss’ Law for Magnetic Fields**  
${\Phi }_{B}=\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}=0\ (Gauss'\ law\ for\ magnetic\ fields)$  
There can be no net “magnetic charge” (individual magnetic poles) enclosed by the surface. The simplest magnetic structure that can exist and thus be enclosed by a Gaussian surface is a dipole, which consists of both a source and a sink for the field lines.  
**Spin Magnetic Dipole Moment**  
${\vec{\mu }}_{S}=-\frac{e}{m}\vec{S}$  
An electron has an intrinsic angular momentum called its ***spin angular momentum*** ***S***; associated with this spin is an intrinsic ***spin magnetic dipole moment μS***.

Differences of S from typical angular momenta:

1. S itself cannot be measured. Instead, only its component along an axis can be measured.  
2. A measured component of S is quantized (restricted to certain values); in fact, it always has the same magnitude (no matter which axis is chosen)

Say S is measured along the z axis:  
${S}_{Z}={m}_{S}\frac{h}{2\pi },\ for\ {m}_{s}=\pm \frac{1}{2}$	mS \= ***spin magnetic quantum number***

**Induced Magnetic Fields**  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{s}={\mu }_{0}{\epsilon }_{0}\frac{d{\Phi }_{E}}{dt}\ (Maxwell's\ law\ of\ induction)$  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{s}={\mu }_{0}{\epsilon }_{0}\frac{d{\Phi }_{E}}{dt}+{\mu }_{0}{i}_{enc}\ (Ampere-Maxwell\ law)$  
When there is a current but no change in electric flux (a wire carrying a constant current), the first term on the right side is zero, and the equation reduces to Ampere’s law.  
When there is a change in electric flux but no current (inside or outside the gap of a charging capacitor), the second term on the right side reduces to Maxwell’s law of induction.

**Displacement Current**  
${i}_{d}={\epsilon }_{0}\frac{d{\Phi }_{E}}{dt}\ (displacement\ current)$  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{s}={\mu }_{0}{i}_{d,enc}+{\mu }_{0}{i}_{enc}\ (Ampere-Maxwell\ law,\ rewritten)$  
Relating displacement current and current in a circular capacitor:  
$q={\epsilon }_{0}AE$  
$\frac{dq}{dt}=i={\epsilon }_{0}A\frac{dE}{dt}$  
${i}_{d}={\epsilon }_{0}\frac{d{\Phi }_{E}}{dt}={\epsilon }_{0}\frac{d(EA)}{dt}={\epsilon }_{0}A\frac{dE}{dt}$  
${i}_{d}=i\ (displacement\ current\ in\ a\ capacitor)$  
Thus, we can consider the displacement current id to be simply a continuation of the real current i from one place, across the capacitor gap, to the other plate.

**Find the Induced Magnetic Field**  
$B=(\frac{{\mu }_{0}{i}_{d}}{2\pi {R}^{2}})r\ (inside\ a\ circular\ capacitor)$  
$B=\frac{{\mu }_{0}{i}_{d}}{2\pi r}\ (outside\ a\ circular\ capacitor)$

**Maxwell’s Equations**  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}=\frac{{q}_{enc}}{{\epsilon }_{0}}$			*Gauss’ law for electricity*  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}=0$			*Gauss’ law for magnetism*  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}=-\frac{d{\Phi }_{B}}{dt}$			*Faraday’s law*  
$\oint\limits_{}^{}\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{s}={\mu }_{0}{\epsilon }_{0}\frac{d{\Phi }_{E}}{dt}+{\mu }_{0}{i}_{enc}$	*Ampere-Maxwell law*  
**Oscillations, LC Circuit**

${v}_{C}=(\frac{1}{C})q$		${v}_{C}=time\ varying\ potential\ difference\ across\ capacitor$  
Connect small resistor to analyze current: 		${v}_{R}=iR$  
$\omega =\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\ (block-spring\ system)$  
*q corresponds to x,	1/C corresponds to k,*  
*I corresponds to v,	L corresponds to m.*  
$\omega =\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\ (LC\ Circuit)$  
$U={U}_{B}+{U}_{E}=\frac{L{i}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{q}^{2}}{2C}$  
$\frac{dU}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{L{i}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{q}^{2}}{2C})=Li\frac{di}{dt}+\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt}=0$  
$L\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{C}q=0\ (LC\ Oscillations)$  
$q=Qcos(\omega t+\phi )\ (charge)$		$Q=amplitude\ of\ charge\ variation)$  
$i=\frac{dq}{dt}=-\omega Qsin(\omega t+\phi )\ (current)$  
Amplitude of sinusoidally varying current is $I=\omega Q$  
$i=-Isin(\omega t+\phi )$  
$\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}=-{\omega }^{2}Qcos(\omega t+\phi )$  
$-L{\omega }^{2}Qcos(\omega t+\phi )+\frac{1}{C}Qcos(\omega t+\phi )=0$  
${U}_{E}=\frac{{Q}^{2}}{2C}co{s}^{2}(\omega t+\phi )$  
${U}_{B}=\frac{{Q}^{2}}{2C}si{n}^{2}(\omega t+\phi )$

**Damped Oscillations in an RLC Circuit**  
$\frac{dU}{dt}=Li\frac{di}{dt}=\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt}=-{i}^{2}R$  
$L\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+R\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{1}{C}q=0\ (RLC\ Circuit)$  
$q=Q{e}^{-Rt/2L}cos(\omega 't+\phi )$	$\omega '=\sqrt{{\omega }^{2}-(R/2L{)}^{2}}$  
$U=\frac{{Q}^{2}}{2C}{e}^{-Rt/L}$

**Alternating Current**  
$\epsilon ={\epsilon }_{m}sin{\ \omega }_{d}t$  
Angular frequency wd of the emf is equal to the angular speed with which the loop rotates in  the magnetic field; the phase of the emf is wdt; and the amplitude of the emf is 𝛜m (m stands for maximum).  
$i=I\ sin({\omega }_{d}t-\phi )$  
${\omega }_{d}=driving\ angular\ frequency$	${\omega }_{d}t-\phi =phase$

**AC Circuits**  
**AC Resistors**  
${v}_{R}={V}_{R}\ sin{\omega }_{d}t$  
${i}_{R}=\frac{{v}_{R}}{R}=\frac{{V}_{R}}{R}sin{\omega }_{d}t$  
${V}_{R}={I}_{R}R\ (resistor)$  
**AC Capacitors**  
${v}_{C}={V}_{C}sin{\omega }_{d}t$  
${q}_{C}=C{v}_{C}=C{V}_{C}sin{\omega }_{d}t$  
${i}_{C}=\frac{d{q}_{C}}{dt}={\omega }_{d}C{V}_{C}cos{\omega }_{d}t$  
${X}_{C}=\frac{1}{{\omega }_{d}C}\ (capacitive\ reactance)$  
$cos{\omega }_{d}t=sin({\omega }_{d}t+90°)$  
${i}_{C}=\frac{{V}_{C}}{{X}_{C}}sin({\omega }_{d}t+90°)$  
${i}_{C}={I}_{C}sin({\omega }_{d}t-\phi )$  
${V}_{C}={I}_{C}{X}_{C}\ (capacitor)$  
**AC Inductive Load**  
${v}_{L}={V}_{L}sin{\omega }_{d}t$  
${v}_{L}=L\frac{d{i}_{L}}{dt}$  
$\frac{d{i}_{L}}{dt}=\frac{{V}_{L}}{L}sin{\omega }_{d}t$  
${i}_{L}=\int\limits_{}^{}d{i}_{L}=\frac{{V}_{L}}{L}\int\limits_{}^{}sin{\omega }_{d}t\ dt=-(\frac{{V}_{L}}{{\omega }_{d}L})cos{\omega }_{d}t$  
${X}_{L}={\omega }_{d}L\ (inductive\ reactance)$  
${i}_{L}=(\frac{{V}_{L}}{{X}_{L}})sin({\omega }_{d}t-90°)$  
${i}_{L}={I}_{L}sin({\omega }_{d}t-90°)$  
${i}_{L}={I}_{L}sin({\omega }_{d}t-\phi )$  
${V}_{L}={I}_{L}{X}_{L}\ (inductor)$

| Circuit Element | Symbol | Resistance or Reactance | Phase of the Current | Phase angle | Amplitude Relation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Resistor | R | R | In phase with v\_R | 0$°$ | V\_R=I\_R R |
| Capacitor | C | X\_C=1/\\omega\_d C | Leads v\_C by 90$°$ | \-90$°$ | V\_C=I\_CX\_C |
| Inductor | L | X\_L=\\omega\_d L | Lags v\_L by 90$°$ | \+90$°$ | V\_L=I\_L X\_L |

**Series RLC Circuits**  
${\epsilon }_{m}={{V}_{R}}^{2}+({V}_{L}-{V}_{C}{)}^{2}$  
${\epsilon }_{m}=(IR{)}^{2}+(I{X}_{L}-I{X}_{C}{)}^{2}$  
$I=\frac{{\epsilon }_{m}}{\sqrt{{R}^{2}+({X}_{L}+{X}_{C}{)}^{2}}}$  
$Z=\sqrt{{R}^{2}+({X}_{L}+{X}_{C}{)}^{2}}\ (impedance\ defined)$  
$I=\frac{{\epsilon }_{m}}{Z}$  
$I=\frac{{\epsilon }_{m}}{\sqrt{{R}^{2}+({\omega }_{d}L-1/{\omega }_{d}C{)}^{2}}}\ (current\ amplitude)$  
$tan\phi =\frac{{V}_{L}-{V}_{C}}{{V}_{R}}=\frac{I{X}_{L}-I{X}_{C}}{IR}$  
$tan\phi =\frac{{X}_{L}-{X}_{C}}{R}\ (phase\ constant)$

**X\_L \> X\_C:** the circuit is said to be ***more inductive than capacitive***. \\phi is positive for such a circuit, which means that phasor \\epsilon\_m rotates ahead of phasor I.  
**X\_C \> X\_L:** the circuit is said to be ***more capacitive than inductive***. \\phi is negative for such a circuit, which means that phasor \\epsion\_m rotates behind phasor I.  
**X\_C \= X\_L:** the circuit is said to be in ***resonance***. \\phi \= 0 for such a circuit, which means that phasors \\epsilon\_m and I rotate together.  
**Resonance**  
${\omega }_{d}L=\frac{1}{{\omega }_{d}C}$  
${\omega }_{d}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\ (maximum\ I)$  
${\omega }_{d}=\omega =\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\ (resonance)$  
**Power**  
$P={i}^{2}R=[Isin({\omega }_{d}t-\phi ){]}^{2}R={I}^{2}Rsi{n}^{2}({\omega }_{d}t-\phi )$  
${P}_{av}=\frac{{I}^{2}R}{2}=(\frac{I}{\sqrt{2}}{)}^{2}R$  
${I}_{rms}=\frac{I}{\sqrt{2}}\ (rms\ current)$  
${P}_{av}={{I}_{rms}}^{2}R\ (average\ power)$  
${V}_{rms}=\frac{V}{\sqrt{2}}\ ;\ {\epsilon }_{rms}=\frac{{\epsilon }_{m}}{\sqrt{2}}(rms\ voltage;\ rms\ emf)$  
${P}_{av}={\epsilon }_{rms}{I}_{rms}cos\phi \ (average\ power)$  
**Transformer**  
${V}_{s}={V}_{P}\frac{{N}_{s}}{{N}_{P}}\ (transformation\ of\ voltage)$  
${I}_{s}={I}_{P}\frac{{N}_{P}}{{N}_{s}}\ (transformation\ of\ currents)$  
${R}_{eq}=(\frac{{N}_{p}}{{N}_{s}}{)}^{2}R$
